speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. I understand that there have been some questions about the statement that I made in the House about the previous question. I would like to clarify that statement for the benefit of Hon. Members. On June 21 I did say that the motion on the previous question is not closure because, after the House votes on the previous question, the debate on the main question will, of course, be resumed. I should have added that it will be resumed, but only if that order is revived.
I would like to quote from the study in the procedural paper which we have prepared on the previous question, explaining what the previous question is all about. It states, "It is designed to limit debate, since until it is decided, it precludes all amendment to the main question."
That is the second point I had made on June 21, that is, that when the previous question is put, this is done only in order to prevent the proposing of new amendments, and that is the exact object of the previous question, to preclude further amendment and to deal immediately with the motion. If carried, thus resolving that the original question be now put, it forces the House to an immediate decision on the main question, in accordance with Standing Order 56(2), which states:
If the previous question be resolved in the affirmative, the original question is to be put forthwith without any amendment or debate.
I hope this clarifies the statement that I made in the course of some points of order, I believe, which were raised on the previous question.

I rise on a point of clarification, Madam Speaker. We were in fact wondering about your remarks and trying to relate them to the rules. In other words, this form of closure that the Government is using will mean that, immediately after the vote on the previous question, Your Honour will then call the vote on second reading unless, of course, the Government should reconsider and negative the vote on the previous question.
If there should be a change of heart on this closure matter, and the Government should vote against the motion of the Hon. Member, which was not moved by an Hon. Member on the front benches, if it were in fact to change its mind and
negative the motion, Your Honour is saying that second reading debate would then be revived the next day and that at that point there would be a chance for further debate. However, the way it stands now, if the Government votes for closure by approving the motion, it will then cut off debate.
[DOT] (ii10)

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Well, that is where I think the Hon. Member has been a bit responsible for the confusion by calling the previous question "closure".
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Be fair. I was answering the matter of closure in my remarks rather than really explaining what the previous question was, so that is why the statement was not complete. What the Hon. Member says is right; if the matter of the previous question is resolved in the affirmative, then we proceed to take action on the main motion.
Thank you very much for the clarification, Madam Speaker. I am sure the people of Canada will call it closure.
Oh, oh!

Briefly, Madam Speaker, last evening after the taking of the vote a question arose regarding whether the vote was accurate or not. I wonder if you would be kind enough to take into consideration that, if a point of order arises out of the vote itself, the vote is not complete until the point of order has been heard and ruled upon, notwithstanding the time of day.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Well, you have to accommodate and adjust several Standing Orders. The point of order was raised once the vote proceeding was finished.
Well, we were trying to-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Yes. When the result of the vote had been given, everything seemed to be terminated as far as the Chair was concerned. Then the point of order was raised. The Chair assumed, perhaps wrongly, but since it was past eleven o'clock, the Chair assumed that the point of order was dealing with something else. That is not surprising because several points of order had been brought up during the day.
The Chair has the responsibility to move the House from one proceeding to the other. In all fairness to the Members who wanted to participate in the adjournment debate, at eleven o'clock the Chair had to give these Members that time. The Chair did not want to take away any of their time. Therefore, at eleven o'clock, since I assumed the point of order would be

June 22, 1983
Business of the House
about something else, not about the vote-the vote was finished and it seemed all right-the Chair protected the three Members who were to speak after eleven o'clock.
The Member's point is well taken, but he also has to remember that once a proceeding is started it is not to be interrupted, and that goes for votes. The voting procedure, once it has started, should not really be interrupted, and the Hon. Member will remember we did have a problem with that at some point.

Madam Speaker, 1 would not want anyone to take my raising this as in any way a criticism of the way it was handled. My concern is that we should know the procedure to follow. I can understand that at the adjournment hour, whatever it is, there is confusion. My only concern is that I want it to be clear that, if there is a point of order arising out of the taking of the vote, the vote is not complete until after the point of order has been heard. 1 think that is what the Chair said.
The timing is sometimes very difficult because it is almost impossible to be heard on a point of order until the Chair has heard the vote. We cannot tell how many people have voted one way or the other until the announcement is made. Therefore we cannot tell whether the totals the Chair has added up include the Member who voted improperly, or not. My only point is that in order to deal with it in a fair and equitable way, we must wait until the announcement of the vote takes place to determine whether the Chair has included the Member or Members who have voted improperly, before we can legitimately raise the point of order that someone voted who should not have done so. Therefore we must raise it after the announcement because, if it were done prior to the announcement, we would be prejudging whether or not that Member had been counted.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
That is perfectly true. However, I must tell the Hon. Member that in the course of proceedings upon taking the vote I could not allow any points of order. The Chair must wait until that proceeding is completed. That is what we did last night.
The Hon. Member is raising a point which 1 recognize and take into account. I do not think it is necessary to expound a principle on this. The Chair always listens to points of order. At any rate, had I not listened to points of order last night past eleven o'clock, we could have dealt with it again this morning. We could have had the record of the vote corrected. It was not definitive because something could have been done about it. It was neater to have done it last night, and I thank the Hon. Members who raised the point last night.

The House resumed, from Tuesday, June 21, 1983, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pepin that Bill C-155, an Act to facilitate the transportation, shipping and handling of western grain and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport, and the Motion of Mr. Lachance (p. 26521).
Mr. Speaker, consensus or closure-

speechtext:
Order. There is no such list, either formally or informally. The Table officers are at the disposal of the Chair. They are the advisers of the Chair. While they may well establish certain lists from time to time to assist the Chair as to who has spoken and who may want to

speak, that in no way should be regarded as an official list. I trust the Parliamentary Secretary appreciates that point. It has no formal standing in the House. The only list by which Hon. Members ought to be guided is the list of speakers printed in Hansard every day.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order on this last comment made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Government House Leader. I think he owes an apology to the Table because hie is impugning people who cannot speak back. I think that is most improper in this assembly.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I appreciate the Hon. Member's assistance. The Chair does not feel slighted in any way.
No, the Table.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Or the Table. The Chair dealt with the matter of the Table officers. These incidents may happen. I think the Chair owed an explanation to the Parliamentary Secretary and to the whole House. I hope that situation is clear for the future. I do not think there was any undue or harsh reflection on the Table officers. I am sure it was not meant that way.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, just to clarify the matter, I am in no way reflecting upon the Table whatsoever. I simply mentioned that I had gone by a list which had been provided by them. I am not suggesting that it has any official status. If the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) would like to look at this list, if he would like me to table it, I would be happy to do so. 1 am casting no reflections whatsoever. I think it was a misunderstanding that has been cleared up. For anyone to cast aspersions on anybody in this matter would be unfortunate and unnecessary.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: May I have one final say on this matter? It is obvious that Hon. Members from time to time seek assistance or direction from the Table officers who are extremely happy and glad to co-operate and be helpful. But Hon. Members should be very careful in their remarks regarding the Table officers. They are not part of the debate. Their conduct is not a matter for reflection. The Chair deals with those matters, and 1 hope that we can now proceed with the debate.

Mr. Speaker, you will notice that I started off my remarks by referring to consensus or closure. I did that for a reason. I anticipated the Parliamentary Secretary or someone else might raise a question, and I wanted to put at least that much of my speech on the record in the event that a decision might be rendered otherwise.
However, I thank the Parliamentary Secretary at this particular time for rising. If there was ever any doubt in anybody's mind as to whether or not this was closure, his intervention indicating that I no longer have any right to speak
Western Grain Transportation Act
indicates to me, and to anyone else listening to or reading my remarks, that he was under the impression I could no longer speak. That, to me, is closure. They cut off speaking. They cut off the possibility for amendment. That is closure.
There are different forms of closure in the House, as the Parliamentary Secretary well knows, having studied the rules very carefully. He has tried to make use of them from time to time. There is such a thing as agreed timing. There was no agreement from this side that we should cut off debate.
What was the one intervention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in this whole debate? It was a notice of motion for closure.
Shame!

The Minister of Agriculture is cutting off spokesmen for people involved in agriculture by saying that we will close off debate at a particular point. What form it was to take, he did not indicate, but the form that was taken now is a pretty good indication-
Louder.

I might have to speak louder for it to sink in. I hope it does. Eventually it will, I can assure you. I can vouch for that. The Hon. Member makes smart-aleck remarks at this point. That is the only kind of interjection he makes. I often wonder why the Members opposite, the bulk of whom are from Quebec, are so silent. Do they not know anything about the subject? Is that why the Member asks me to speak louder? Those Members do not even sit in the House. They just take off and flock in at the time of a vote. They flock around their Leader.
Is there no one opposite who will take up the challenge to debate? We had an interjection from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) who said that they would impose closure. Is that an indication that there is consensus? This Government promised it would not move on the Crow until there was a consensus. We have now reached the point where the Government is imposing closure. Is that consensus?
Do you, Mr. Speaker, feel that we should not introduce any further amendments? Do you feel that the issue is not large enough? Do you think this is only a regional problem? It affects the West Coast and it affects the Prairies. I often wonder why they call it the Prairies, because we have a lot of forests, rivers, and so on. It also affects central Canada, Quebec, and the Maritimes. It has very broad implications.
Quebec Members were very disturbed in the past that the Government was going to move on the Crow. What has silenced them? Did any one of them rise and give us an indication why they will support closure? The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) owes the Members of this House and all Canadians an explanation. What is he going to do? Where are we moving to? What guarantee do we have from the Government if we move by closure-and I repeat closure-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I wish the Hon. Member would check Hansard, because Madam Speaker ruled very clearly that this motion was in order and that it was not a closure motion. Madam Speaker made that very clear. The Hon. Member can check that in Hansard.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: That is not a point of order. We are proceeding with debate. That is a matter of opinion at this stage.

A rose by any other name would smell as sweet. When historians look back at this debate, they will ask what happened to the Crow. They will ask whether, after 85 years, it died of old age or because it was no longer of any use. History will record that the Crow was choked. Debate on the Crow was choked. It can be called choking, or it can be called closure. I will call it closure. I will tell the people of Canada that it is closure, because that is what it is. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Flis) confirmed that. Closure is taking place even though many, many problems will arise.
To attend this debate which began last week, I had to absent myself from a hearing on rail line abandonment. Rail line abandonment was occurring simultaneously with the attempt to change the Crow to charge the farmer more for transporting grain.
In addition to paying a higher price for moving grain from a point further from their farms, farmers will have to deal with rail line abandonment. If you can believe it, Mr. Speaker, a 13-mile long rail line will be abandoned so that CN would then have to transfer grain an extra 146 miles to get to the same point. Now that is economy! If anyone thinks that we have no reason to continue debating this question, think again, because that is precisely what is happening in the West.
That extra mileage charge that the farmer must add to his cost of operation, is that part of the blending formula of which the Minister speaks? The Minister does not speak. He owes it to the House to tell us whether or not he has made a deal with Members of the NDP. Members of the NDP kept telling us that the Conservatives were making a deal that would make paying either the farmer or the railway optional. What kind of a deal has been cooked up with Members of the NDP? We thought they said they were opposed to it. Now we hear on the CBC that they have made a deal. I wonder what is going on over there between those two. Now who is making the deal, and what are they making a deal for? I thought they were opposed to it. If they are opposed to it, then there is no deal. But what was all that about? The Minister owes it to the House to tell us whether there is or was a deal, or whether there will be a deal with the NDP. What is going on?
Last night we heard from the agricultural spokesman for the NDP. We had to root him out a little bit, but he got up. He was up, but he never commented on the kind of wheeling and dealing that was going on.
With the man with the green hat.

Yes, someone has mentioned the man with the green hat. Instead of wearing a green hat, that Minister should be wearing an engineer's cap from now on. He went to Winnipeg to meet with the rail people there. They all gleefully rubbed their hands together and took a few wonderful pictures, and the people from the railway said, "Well, it is not quite good enough, but it is a step in the right direction." They said this as they smiled all the way to the bank. Of course they should smile because of the guaranteed income, and because Members of the NDP are making deals.
The Minister should change his hats occasionally, I think, if only in the interest of sanitation. Outside of that, I think that maybe an engineer's cap would suit him well.
I think that if the Minister goes to the West he might find out what effect the actions of the Government will have on the West. We in the West have no cost guarantees. We have no guarantees on what the railways will do with their books. Who will inspect those books? What will be the costs?

Mr. Speaker, I too rise today to add my remarks to the debate on the motion to call the previous question which, by any other term, is clearly closure, because when we vote on this we must move immediately to the main motion on second reading, and that is the end of it.
There has been much debate over this issue, Sir, but I think it is clear that everyone has been trying to convince Government Members to change their views with respect to Bill C-155. I shall try to do this by showing them that it is simply improper within the Canadian context. Bill C-155 is not the Canadian way to solve the problem.
I am sure that Government Members realize that this Party is trying to represent the broad range of views and interests which a Bill like this must reflect. For example, there are the grain producers. The amendments that we fought for, such as the safety net and the removal of the cap, were designed to protect the legitimate interests of the grain producers in the West. But there are other legitimate interests in the West because the West is not a homogeneous, one product region.
There is also the livestock industry, the cow-calf producers, Canadian men and women who own their own farms. There are feedlot operators and other good Canadians who pay their
June 22, 1983

fair share of taxes and more. There are the livestock processors and there are also those who grow specialty crops, Mr. Speaker.
We seem to think that this Bill will automatically cover all grain in the West. Well, it will not. It covers only Canadian Wheat Board crops, of which there are only six. A few more have been added, but there are many specialty crops that are not covered. Canadian farmers, people who have been in Canada for four and five generations and who have put their whole lives and hearts and souls into the country, will be blocked because of this Bill. They will be blocked because the process is wrong, Mr. Speaker.
We stand for the future. We recognize that there will be changes, and therefore we have addressed our attention to seeing that those changes are made with the best interests of the West and, therefore, of the whole country at heart, because as the regions are strong the whole country will be strong. In this country, there is no reason why every region cannot be strong. The Atlantic region with its fisheries and forests and minerals, Quebec with its enormous hydro-electric power, Ontario with its manufacturing base, and the West with its millions and millions of acres of land and the water that flows from the mountains, these regions can all be strong. We can produce food and livestock, Mr. Speaker, for the entire world. We have barely tapped our potential. Yet this Bill will block that potential, and the Liberal and NDP strategy to put this Bill through will just finish it off.
Contrast our position with that of the NDP, Mr. Speaker. Members of the NDP only really represent one group, the National Farmers' Union. That is a small group of farmers. There are over 150,000 farmers in the West; the NFU, as I recall, has about 3,000 to 3,500 members. When I saw the books of the NFU two years ago, it was $750,000 in debt. It cannot even run its own organization properly, just like the Liberals who are running the country. They both have debts that are truly enormous.
What else have Members of the NDP done about this, Mr. Speaker? They have been betraying the West since 1980. The constitutional proposal was a direct attack on the West, and NDP Members backed it. The National Energy Program was a direct attack upon Canadian companies, upon people who are building the nation and paying taxes to try to make Canada a world power in terms of economic strength and feeding the world, and they backed that Bill. We have since seen the decline and the absolute demise of the oil industry in the West.
What about Canagrex? In spite of the fact that we have had the experience of VIA Rail as a Crown corporation, the experience of Canadair, which is costing union labourers $1.5 billion, the experience of de Havilland-
What about the Wheat Board?

I could talk about the Wheat Board if the Hon. Member wants to deal with it. What about Petro-Canada? That corporation has cost Canadians about $7 billion.
Western Grain Transportation Act
What has that to do with the Crow?

Ordinary citizens, Mr. Speaker, have difficulty accepting the fact that they have less money in their pockets and less disposable income because of the over 300 Crown corporations. Yet Members of the New Democratic and Liberal Parties got together and created another Crown corporation for agriculture.
Sir, this Bill represents a problem for the West solely because of inflation. At one half cent per ton mile for 70 years, the railways made money, the grain people made money, and there was no distortion affecting the livestock industry or, if there was, it was small enough that the industry was able to cope with it, as were the processors. As a result, people made money for 70 years. Then came inflation which we know was caused by the deficits. The Government over-stimulated the economy this year to the extent of $30 billion. Those deficits lead to inflation and high interest rates, which then lead to collapse. This is exactly what was done dozens of times throughout history. It became a serious problem and the Minister, quite properly, put together a group of 60 or 70 of the finest minds in the West, men who work all the time in agriculture, and they came up with the Gilson proposals. Their suggestion was for 81 per cent to the producers and 19 per cent to the railways.
That is true.

Then the Minister came back with his February statement, called the Pepin proposals. They payment was reduced from 81-19 to 50-50. The groups in the West who would suffer under this distortion said that they could live with it. But then an entirely different group of people, the Liberal Quebec caucus, became involved, and politics entered into it. They said the payment must go 100 per cent to the railway. The NDP agreed absolutely; they want 100 per cent of the payment to go to the railways. It amounts to a guaranteed annual income to one of the largest corporations and perhaps the most wealthy corporation in the world. The NDP wants the payment to go there.
The solution to the western problem was arrived at in the West when some of the top minds got together, but because of politics, and because of the Liberal caucus, it was destroyed, and again the NDP is backing the Government.
We must have this Bill changed, Mr. Speaker. I plead with Liberal Members to change their minds. The Department of Agriculture has filed extensive information which shows that a payment to the producers will not adversely affect Quebec. The Minister of Agriculture in Ontario has said that his studies show that it would not affect Ontario either. For the Quebec caucus to direct that payment be made 100 per cent to the railways rather than to the producers, in the face of the document filed by the Minister of Agriculture, which shows that it will have no effect whatsoever, is simply wrong.
I plead with my colleagues opposite to go to work on the Cabinet and have this changed. If that payment is made to the

June 22, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
producers it gives them some freedom of choice. When they deliver their grain or decide what to produce, they may decide not to ship it by railway but by truck. That would mean that hundreds and hundreds of Canadian owned and operated trucking companies will buy trucks manufactured in Ontario. Farmers will haul the grain to the central railway locations, and trains could go back and forth on a rotation of seven days at the most. By removing the cap at the same time, we could export 40 million tonnes of grain.
You want to get rid of the branch lines. You have just admitted it.

Mr. Speaker, the NDP wants to keep every branch line the way it is. Members of that Party forget that the branch lines were designed for the horse and buggy days, when a horse could only walk 4.5 miles and back in a day. That is why there was a town and village every nine miles. Now we have roads and we have trucks which can drive 30 or 40 miles quite easily.
You want to get rid of those towns? Is that what you are saying?

Under the Crow those towns have been going down for years and years. They were designed for the horse and buggy days, but now, with cars and trucks, people are choosing to drive to the larger centres, and there are centres every 30 or 40 miles. That is as natural as growing from a child to an adult, but the NDP is stuck with its adolescent ideology. Members of the NDP dream that if everyone is equal, somehow things are going to be more Christian, more fair. They want equality of result, but we know from the nature of man that some people are smarter, some are more musical than others. No matter what test is applied, some people are better off and some are worse off.
We say that we need a fully competitive system, and that is what the payment to the producer will bring about, Mr. Speaker. It will bring true competition to the West. If a railway gets out of line people will just switch to trucks, to pipelines or anything else, in the future. In that way we will ensure the most efficient operation because the bottom line is that we have to put a bushel of grain at tidewater competitive to the United States, Argentina, and Australia. Those countries are whipping us, Mr. Speaker. If we follow the logic of the NDP and the Liberals, we will be in the dark ages forever.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak because I have a particular interest in this Bill. There is an aspect of it which has not been given much attention, and that is its effect on Crown lands. This aspect has been completely ignored in the debate. I am surprised to find that the Government of British Columbia has indicated in a variety of ways that it would be very favourably disposed toward Members of the House from British Columbia who would agree that the Bill should go through.
In the mail I received the text of a statement made by the Minister of Transportation and Highways for the Province of
British Columbia when he spoke in Vancouver about Bill C-155 and about the length of thus debate. Thanks to the ten-minute speech rule, a variety of aspects of the Bill can be brought to the attention of Canadians, and I think this is important.
We are trying to let it be known from one coast to the other that there are elements of this Bill which are dangerous. No one contests the fact that some changes must be made to the Crow rate. The Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankow-ski) has stated on more than one occasion, and in a variety of places, the principles which guide the approach of this Party to the Bill.
This Bill is meant to ensure that the federal Government and the railways continue to provide a special low rate consistent with the Crowsnest Pass agreement to assist producers to compete with subsidized grain exporting nations. This is essential. Agriculture is the lifeblood of this country. We grew up in an agricultural domain. My parents moved out to central Canada from Nova Scotia in the latter years of the previous century because there was an opportunity there to grow grain. This is what made this country-grain and the railways. They have been inevitably interwoven with our history.
Ndw, not content with destroying Parliament, the Government has decided to destroy the very thing that makes the nation work, the combination of railways and agriculture.
The introduction of closure stinks, Mr. Speaker. Whatever you want to call it, it still stinks. That is what is being imposed, and that is what is destroying this House. When I was first elected it was a place where I felt I could serve with dignity. Because of the disrepute into which the House has fallen as a result of the Government, I am now finding that is almost-1 hesitate to use the word-but it is almost a disgrace to serve in the House. The Government has destroyed Parliament's underpinnings in the procedural sense. Now it is set on destroying the country, and it has done a pretty good job of it up till now in other areas.
We are finding that in the matter of transportation the Government is determined to set East against West. 1 think that is an absolutely shocking performance for any so-called Government of Canada.
Another principle, which is recognized in the Bill but in a different way, is to provide fair compensation to the railways for moving grain in order to provide the necessary capital to maintain new and existing plant and equipment. It must be fair compensation, not total compensation. A full compensatory rate would make our products unsaleable in the world, Mr. Speaker. That is what we must recognize. Because of the size of this country the railways have a public responsibility to ensure that the railroad continues to exist and to serve this country.
I was deeply distressed when the passenger service across this country was eviscerated. That is the best word I can think
June 22, 1983

of. Passenger service was absolutely eviscerated. I saw in something I was reading the other day that VIA Rail is now registering heavy losses. It should still be possible, Mr. Speaker, for people who wish to travel across this country by train to be able to do so. You cannot get any notion of the size of this country unless you are actually on the ground, travelling at normal speed across the land. I am appalled that the transportation system, as far as passengers are concerned, has been so downgraded by the Government. I remember it was a tricky method Government had for introducing VIA Rail. I am wondering if it still has any statutory basis. I rather think it does not. However, that is beside the point.
There is a need for railroads not just to carry our products across the country, but also to carry our people. Those who feel they have no time to spare, that they must fly, do not know what this country is all about. They do not know the extent of the fields on the Prairies because they have not gone through them either in a car or on a train.
The third principle is to guarantee producers an efficient, cost-effective, and reliable grain transportation system. We have all seen those yellow and red cars, the grain tankers, moving across the country. I was absolutely appalled to think that one of the Provinces had to chip in to produce some extra cars, that our rail system had been so downgraded that it could not produce those cars. A single Province, Alberta, had to produce additional cars to carry our grain produce.
There is a need for an efficient, cost-effective, and reliable grain transportation system. There is no question about that. However, Bill C-155 is not the way to do it.
There is a need to remove the distortion of the low freight rates in grain and oilseeds vis-a-vis processed products, and ensure that the natural advantage is retained. This is what has produced a great deal of the opposition in the West to this Bill, because this Bill does not do that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Let's hear your solution.
The best solution that I can think of, Mr. Speaker, since we have heard a muttering from the Hon. Member opposite, is an election right now!
Hear, hear!
That is the solution.

That, of course, is the Maritime Freight Rates Act. That came into existence to help alleviate the justified concern in Atlantic Canada in trying to get an economy going there by its bootstraps. After several royal commissions, it was put into law in 1926.
I was in the House when the then Minister of Transport, the Hon. Don Jamieson, seduced Members to agree to the Atlantic transportation amendment. That was some time in the 1970s. He said that would be the first plank in a revised transportation policy for Atlantic Canada which would make Atlantic Canada grow. It was the beginning of the whittling away of the effects, help and assistance and the subsidy for Atlantic industry in the select territory.
A month or so ago this Minister, his Department and some advisers, who very poorly advised, unilaterally set up a commission of consultants from Ottawa to assess the viability of even continuing the Maritime Freight Rates Act. All I can say in the closing 30 seconds available to me is that people in western Canada have justified concern about what is being done to the Crow, their pillar, as the pillar that we have had since 1926 is being slowly whittled away. If the terms of reference of the consultants' report are met, I predict-but hopefully there will be an election first-that it will be the serious intent of this Minister or his replacement, as long as this Government is in office, to ensure that the Maritime Freight Rates Act, let alone the At and East rates for the export of flour on which there has already been one attack, will go out the window.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to say a few words in connection with Bill C-155. Bill C-155 is a great betrayal, the betrayal of half a nation. On February 8, 1982 the Hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) said in his western rail transportation statement under item 5:
The economic distortions within the agricultural sector stemming from the statutory rate should be reduced-
Under item 6 of the same statement, he said further:
The most effective ways of promoting the diversification of the western agricultural economy and processing of agricultural products-
So he spent $287,000 and more to set up a committee with those statements as the terms of reference. Mr. Gilson and, as one of my colleagues noted, some of the best brains in Canada came up with a solution. The Minister should have accepted that solution. He did accept it at first. Then he cut it in half and then he threw it out altogether. This is the greatest betrayal of half the nation in Canadian history.
Judas betrayed Christ for 30 pieces of silver. He paid for it. I want to tell the Hon. Minister that he will pay for this betrayal and the Liberal Party will pay for it. It is proper that they should pay, but the Canadian people will pay for this as well, particularly the people of western Canada.
I want to deal with some of the items in this great betrayal by the Minister. If the Minister were a man of principle, he would resign from his position. If he believed what he set out in the terms of reference and then he backed out and turned his back on those promises, he should resign. If he is half a man, he should resign. But no, he sits there. His position is more important than our country. That is what this Bill is all about. This Bill will either make the country or destroy it. The way the Bill is set up now, it could well destroy the country. It is a great betrayal.
As for my hon. friends from the NDP, there has been a great sell-out. They speak up against the Bill and then they turn around and say: "Now we will pay it to the railways, not to the farmers".

He wants the formula for the people of Canada so that the people can decide.
When Members of the NDP oppose that proposition, they oppose people. Have they no confidence in the people? The people of the country are not illiterate, they are well educated. The farmers are well educated, but the NDP cannot trust the people to decide what is best for themselves. Their philosophy is to tell the people what is good for them, and that is the philosophy of the Liberal Government as well. It has been telling the people what is good for them for years. That is coming to an end because the people are getting tired of it. The people want some say.
The freedom of choice proposition will give the people a chance to say whether they want the money to go to the railway, as some will. It is their right to say so. If they do want the money to go to the railway, those people will get a card that will indicate the rate that is appropriate for that particular situation. There are other people who will say they want the money to go into their own pockets because they know how to spend the money better than does the Government. They
will not waste it. They may want to use the money to haul feed to a feedlot where they are doing wonderful work. They may want to use it to feed hogs or use it for a pulse crop. An official of the CPR, when he came to visit me, said: "We favour seeing the money go into the pockets of the producers". I said: "You do?" He said: "Yes, I do, because that will make our railway more efficient. We will have to compete, and in order to compete we will have to be efficient." They do not mind blocking hog producers who have a tremendous potential. They do not mind killing the cattle industry when it has been making money and has a tremendous potential. Madam Speaker, the Canadian International Development Agency has been without a president for almost a year. Recently Ms. Margaret Catley-Carlson was appointed to the position. The new President comes with a good deal of experience in the field of international aid.
As Ms. Catley-Carlson prepares to take over her new job, I would suggest to her that she consider carefully some recent reports on Canadian aid published by the North-South Institute in Ottawa. The Institute criticizes the Canadian foreign aid program because it has not been allowed to develop clear, practical goals.
Foreign aid is a very difficult activity. This I know from my own experience. All Canadian experience acquired over the years must now be used to define a clear direction. The last guidelines for CIDA were laid out for the period 1975-80. This past year, even without new guidelines and without a president, aid programs have continued.
CIDA is beginning to take on the look and attitude of a middle-aged person. The wonderment of childhood is gone, the excitement of youth is over, the hard knocks of young adulthood have taken their toll, and the institution is showing signs of middle-age fatigue. I call upon the new President of CIDA to take to heart the advice of the North-South Institute, first, to decentralize decision-making; second, to speed up procedures of decision making by placing more staff in the field with more authority; and third, to remember that aid is for the poor so that aid given quickly is aid given twice.

Madam Speaker, the large majority of the Canadian people want the death sentence restored for anyone deliberately planning and then murdering another human being, when he or she has been found guilty beyond the shadow of a doubt. Under this formula there is no chance of the wrong person being executed. Still, Liberal Members continually refer to persons where there is or was a doubt; if there is a doubt, the law would remain as it is today.
One Liberal Member calls capital punishment revenge. It is not revenge; it is just and proper punishment to fit the crime. Some way the death sentence is not a deterrent. Well, it would certainly stop a murderer from committing a second or a third or a fourth murder. Maybe nothing would stop a murder carried out in a fit of passion, but it would certainly prevent some murders that are coolly planned. Why? Because everyone loves life and has no desire to die.
Parents of murdered young people, like Walter and Marion Cook, whose beautiful teenaged daughter, Kelly, was brutally murdered, and the loved ones of the two girls killed by Peters and Brown, know what it is to go through torment and hell, and want the murderers executed to make sure such a horrible ordeal does not happen to some other family.
But the Government thinks it knows more than the people; it refuses to reflect the thinking of the people; it insists on telling the people what it considers is good for them, and so murderers will go on murdering a second and third and fourth time, until a democratic Government that will reflect the thinking of the people, is elected.

Madam Speaker, national security is a top priority in every nation's hierarchy of values. We Canadians treasure our sovereignty above all, and will not let any alien forces infiltrate our lives. In the era of spy networks operating ruthlessly all over the world, we must be particularly vigilant. Therefore a strong and efficient security agency is of prime importance for our defence, and every effort should be made to allow our spy chasers to do their job. Yet, in doing so, we must not forget about one of the greatest achievements of our system-the rule of law.
It is imperative that no one, not even the Security Service, should be permitted to break the law. Bill C-157, as proposed, poses a threat to our civil liberties, the integrity of democracy, and natural justice.
An increasing number of letters from my constituents, voicing their opposition to this legislation, indicates clearly where Canadians stand when it comes to attacks on our freedoms and the rule of law. They demand assurance on the part of the security forces that no abuses of law, as known in the past, will ever take place, and that their personal freedoms will not be endangered. A careful and detailed review of the legislation is needed so that both the requirements of our national interests are met and our personal freedoms preserved.

Madam Speaker, the Winnipeg Construction Association has contacted me expressing concern at the manner in which federal public works contracts are handled. It would seem that the Association is not given adequate advance notice when a project is to begin, and often the specifics of projects are not readily available. Therefore, they cannot be fully prepared-a necessary prerequisite in order to organize and establish the detailed planning essential to beginning and completing every new project, and tendering. I am referring in particular to the expansion and modernization of the Winnipeg airport, a new project recently announced by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), which will cost $32 million.
This news is most exciting for, as a rule, the weekly public works communique lists Manitoba as not being awarded any contracts, regardless of my continuous pursuit of the Minister of Employment to utilize the fine workmanship of Manitobans.
1 am pleased that, after all these years, he is beginning to realize that my commendation of Manitobans and their multitude of skills and talents is not unfounded.
I would ask that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. LeBlanc) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration endeavour to supply the Winnipeg Construction Association with all the detailed information on the airport renovation project, as well as attempt on a regular basis to inform the Association as auickly as possible of any upcoming public works contracts, as is done by provincial Governments.

Madam Speaker, the CNR is threatening the life of the Towhship of Nakina, Ontario, by proposing to eliminate Nakina as a crew-change point and to run trains right through. This will have a devastating impact on the community as the proposed run-through will deprive it of its oldest industry, namely, the CNR, and make it into a one industry forestry town with all the economic instability that results from such dependence.
In addition, the run-through will cause many families to move out of Nakina, and leave the remaining residents, many of them senior citizens, to pay for all the new services and infrastructure the CNR encouraged the town to build. The people of Nakina were assured by the CNR that they had a secure future and, as a result, many families built or purchased homes in Nakina which would be radically devalued if the CNR goes ahead with the Nakina run-through.
The people of Nakina would like to remain there and to preserve their community. They quite rightly feel the CNR has an obligation to allow them to do this. It is time the CNR, as a Crown corporation, acted in the public interest and cancelled the proposed Nakina run-through so that the people of that community can continue to live and work there without fear of losing their homes, their friends, their community, and their lifestyles.
To those who like to say, as do many of my Liberal and Conservative colleagues, that you cannot stop progress, I say that the destruction of communities is not progress at all. It is an illusion of progress behind which we find the erosion of values and relationships which really count.

Madam Speaker, men and women who are privileged to live in a free and democratic society have an obligation and a responsibility to speak out against violations of human rights, wherever they occur in the world. We must do so because those who are the victims of oppression and terror are seldom in a position to make a public plea on their own behalf. Such is the case with thousands of victims of senseless killings in Central America, as it is with brave dissidents who dare to speak out in Iron Curtain countries. We saw another brutal example of oppression in these past few days against defenceless human beings. Once again members of the Baha'i faith in Iran have been executed for their beliefs by the Government of that country.
The Baha'is have been subjected to incredible harassment and torture by the followers of Ayatollah Khomeini. Since he seized power, 130 Baha'i leaders have been executed by the Government. This past week ten women of the Baha'i faith were executed in Iran simply for teaching children the basic tenets of their religion. Peoples and Governments around the world must protest these savage and outrageous acts of violence until the rights of Baha'is to live in peace and security, free to practise their religion, are respected.

two-thirds of Manitoba, an area which is very highly dependent on air transportation. 2. Yes, the Department of National Health and Welfare has sponsored reviews of Canadian and foreign data relating to safety and effectiveness of analgesics by Expert Advisory Committees composed of nongovernment pharmacologists and clinicians on a number of occasions during the 1970s and 1980s.

Mr. Speaker, another feature of the freedom of choice concept is that it hurts nobody. It does not hurt the railways. It puts the railways in a position that if they give good service, the people will use the railways. The more efficient the railways become, the more money they would make. That is the proper way for a free enterprise project to work.
It will not hurt the farmers of Quebec. The farmers of Quebec will still have their markets and will still have their own subsidies. Freedom of choice for western Canadians will not hurt the Quebec people. It will not hurt anybody.
It will not hurt the Government. As a matter of fact, it will be of benefit to the Government because it will allow the Government to show that it is democratic by getting back to the people and letting the people decide some of these things. The freedom of choice proposition has tremendous possibilities.
Freedom of choice would be beneficial to every farm family home in western Canada because the husband and wife and children could decide what is best for them and how they want to use the money. The people will have the say. That is a wonderful concept, and I would like to see it adopted by the Government. It would be to its credit to adopt it.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak on this very important legislation, Bill C-155. At the same time, I am pleased to pay tribute to the outstanding contributions which have been made by my colleagues, in particular the Hon. Members for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) and Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), who have done such an outstanding job in communicating to the people of Canada the position taken by the New Democratic Party on this very important legislation.
I would like to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that this issue does not affect only one region of the country. This issue is of national importance. Even though the Crow rate has effectively been described as the Magna Carta of the West, in many ways the ramifications of this Bill go far beyond the West. I as a representative of a constituency in British Columbia have a number of very serious concerns about the effect this Bill would have on my constituents. I know that in the course of this debate my colleagues have tried to bring forth the concerns they have as to how the Bill might affect not only their constituents but people all across the country.
I would note as well that we are faced with a very important question of process when dealing with this legislation. It has been suggested, in effect, that there has been enough debate. Parliament is being gagged and muzzled by the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Rosemont (Mr. Lachance) which would effectively deny us any opportunity to improve this legislation in principle at second reading. Any possible amendments are being presented. There were a number of amendments we suggested which we believed would have improved this legislation, but through a parliamentary device which was last used in the House, I believe, in 1955 we are being stifled and debate is in effect being closed. This kind of back door closure and trickery is completely unacceptable.
We have heard the Official Opposition talk about freedom of choice. In many respects, for the farmer freedom of choice means freedom to choose how he or she is to be shafted by the PC proposals. Effectively, there are no safeguards whatsoever to ensure that the farming community will not be very badly hurt by the legislation. We have seen estimates which show that some $6,000 per year will be lost by the average farmer. The Government has the nerve to suggest that he should accept that and that this debate should be ended. That is not acceptable, Mr. Speaker.
I have noted that this is an issue of national importance. I should like to draw the attention of the House to a statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) primarily in western Canada with respect to this legislation. He said that he was hearing different views on the Crow rate from different groups in the West and that he had made it clear that the Government would like to settle the matter in a way which would achieve the greatest possible consensus in the West.
There is far from being a consensus in the West, Mr. Speaker. This is one of the most divisive pieces of legislation ever seen in western Canada. On February 13, 1981 the Prime Minister said that at the present time it was the Government's policy not to touch the Crow rate, but if there was a general feeling in the West that the question must be reopened, then it would be happy to do so.
Not only is there not a general feeling in the West that the Crow rate should be reopened, but in fact the general feeling in the West is quite to the contrary. The Government of Saskatchewan, the Government of Manitoba and the Government of Alberta were not quite sure where they stood. Certainly they have been rather silent on this important issue although they have been vociferous on other questions, such as that of dismantling medicare in Alberta.
I should like to deal with some of the particular concerns that Members from British Columbia have about the legislation. I would preface my remarks by saying that it is rather curious that in this bonanza for the CPR-and that is what it is, a bonanza for the CPR-there is no suggestion there be a quid pro quo. It might be one thing if we were to be told that the poor, suffering CPR was finally going to be adequately compensated for transporting grain if in exchange, as a quid pro quo, it were to turn Marathon Realty over to the people of Canada. But we do not hear anything about the profit-making subsidiaries of CP Rail, Mr. Speaker.
Last year this corporate giant had a profit of $485 million on assets over $16 billion, so the silence is rather curious in view of the suggestion that a bargain was made with the people of Canada, particularly with the farmers in western Canada. That bargain is being broken with this legislation. That sacred trust with the farmers of western Canada and indeed with this country is being broken. In exchange for an agreement to transport grain at the statutory rate, CP Rail was given vast tracts of land, mineral rights and money.
It has been suggested that if CP were suddenly to renege on the bargain, the taxpayers of Canada have the right to insist that the resources involved be put into the hands of the people of Canada. I have heard very little about this from Members of the Official Opposition and Members of the Government. As we know very well, both Parties receive very significant corporate contributions from CP Rail, so perhaps that is why the old saying "He who pays the piper expects to call the tune" is appropriate in his case.
It has been suggested that shippers of other products in British Columbia might pay more as a result of the Crow rate, but that is not so, Mr. Speaker. To change the Crow rate will not in any way relax the freight rate screw on other shippers. The railways are in a monopoly position in western Canada and will set their rate at whatever the market will bear. In any event, the transportation of grain accounts for only 13 per cent of total transportation. The Government of Alberta, that great free enterprise Government, admits that the railways would continue to set rates on the historic basis and would not be affected by the increased grain revenues.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have an opportunity to enter the debate on this motion today. I thought it would be a rather lengthy motion so I looked it up on the Order Paper and saw that it is very simple. It reads:
That this question be now put.
Western Grain Transportation Act
It sounds almost insignificant. However, there are a whole lot of implications in this one short sentence. Knowing my good friend, the Hon. Member who introduced the motion, as usual what he says has hidden implications.
This sentence gives me some concern because essentially what we are doing with that short phrase is moving into closure. We are cutting off debate. It is not the usual closure motion, but in fact that is simply what it accomplishes. There will be no room for further amendments. Therefore, any hope we had for discussion on various aspects of the Crow Bill is cut off. There is no chance for further debate on issues like the freedom of choice option which has been put forward by the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). There is no assurance at this point that we, as an Opposition and as Hon. Members, in my case from the West, who are particularly concerned about this Bill and the effect of the legislation, have really been heard yet by the Minister. As a result of the motion, we do have some concerns because what in fact we are facing is closure.
The question I suppose then is: Why do we have closure at this particular time? The Government is always going to say that a Government has a right to legislate. It has the right to pass its laws, to introduce them into the House, and to make sure that those laws are debated and passed through the legislative process. We know that the Standing Orders of the House do make considerable reference to that opportunity. A great deal of the Standing Orders are put in place precisely for that purpose.
Of course, that is the viewpoint of the Government on that particular issue. However, on the other side of the coin, one principle which I believe is equally important is the viewpoint of the Opposition and its right-you might even say its duty- to oppose legislation in the hopes of obtaining improvement, to oppose legislation in the hopes of bringing to light some of the flaws that we as an Opposition see in a particular piece of legislation. Just as there are Standing Orders on the one side to allow the Government to proceed with its legislation, there are also Standing Orders on the other side to allow the Opposition the full and complete opportunity to oppose, to enter into debate and to discuss and report legislation. Therefore, those provisions are of equal importance to the Government's purpose. They also serve a very significant purpose in what happens in this House and what happens to legislation, and ultimately what we hope is good legislation coming through the House of Commons.
The question really boils down to why do we, as an Opposition, want to see an extended, careful, thorough debate on Bill C-155, the Crow legislation? The reason is that we feel it is important. I feel we can essentially look at approximately four particular reasons why we want to see this legislation given a thorough airing. First, it is because of the fact that the Crow is

of fundamental importance, particularly to the West, but having a dramatic effect on all of Canada. That is because it is a long-term program. The Crow rate is a program which has been going on for a long period of time and any changes will have a continued effect for the foreseeable future.
Second, this particular program has been of great benefit to farmers over the years. It has allowed them time for planning, and that has been significant if one looks at many of our farmers in terms of rapidly increasing costs such as fuel, fertilizer, machinery, land, interest, development of land and so on. All those costs become very significant. Something as stable as the Crow benefit over a long period of time has allowed our farmers to plan and has allowed them to do some serious and straightforward thinking.
The farmers in my region are concerned about still having to develop some land. That was one of the original purposes of the Crow benefit. It was to allow our early farmers to be able to bring their agricultural land onstream and to develop it. In Peace River country that is quite an involved process. That means taking trees off the land, taking out the roots and breaking the land, all of which is expensive. There is still a very viable purpose for this in my area because we are still trying to bring on new land. We have a lot of agricultural land left which is tree covered, which is not yet into production. Therefore, the Crow benefit still has that particular benefit to farmers in the Peace River country.
Another reason why I believe it is necessary to have good, clear, concise debate is that the Crow rate is now nearly 100 years old. Surely, when we come into a situation such as we are facing here in the House of Commons now, there should be very little, if any, difficulty in setting aside a few months or a few hours of debate in order to assure that we do what is right to this particular piece of legislation which will have such a dramatic impact on the West and in fact on all of Canada. However, as usual, this Government once again is in a big hurry. It has to rush it through. It has to use closure in whatever form to accomplish its particular interests and goals. It is not concerned about what happens to those who are directly and dramatically affected by this legislation.
Another reason for having a good debate on this particular issue is that the Government does not have any representation in the West. Surely it is not unreasonable to ask that this House take a little time to hear some of the viewpoints which reflect that region of the country which is not represented on the Government's side in this particular legislation. There must be time to entertain amendments because those amendments provide new debate and new discussion and the chance of improving the legislation. There must be time to look at general improvements in the Bill, one of which I referred to earlier in my remarks, the proposal of freedom of choice which was put forward by the Hon. Member for Vegreville.
The whole concept of freedom of choice becomes very significant and very important to people in a region such as I represent simply because we have in so many of our areas large parts of the riding which are not serviced by rail and, therefore, our farmers must load their grain into trucks and travel as much as 100 to 120 miles to the nearest railhead. Therefore,
the possibility of having a choice in terms of how farmers ship their grain and where that Crow benefit would be paid becomes very significant to them. That is one of the issues on which I would like to see a full discussion here in the House of Commons. That could have been very simply done through amendments, through discussions with the Minister and through various debates in the House. Today, however, we see this opportunity coming to an end very simply because of the motion which has been put forward that the question be now put, which is essentially closure, so that the whole debate comes grinding to a halt.
Another reason I believe it is important that we have a good debate is the basic lack of trust in this Government from coast to coast in this country. If one looks at the Gallup polls, one sees that on a national average it has around 30 per cent or 32 per cent support. That is on a national average; in the particular part of the country from which I come it is significantly lower than that. Therefore there is a real basic lack of trust.
Why has that come about? I believe part of the reason has to be because of debate and debating opportunities here in the House of Commons. I can refer to one particular piece of legislation which was railroaded through here not too long ago, the National Energy Program. We saw that piece of legislation, which was so interventionist and had such a dramatic effect on western Canada, forced through the House with very little input from western Members because, obviously, if any Hon. Member from western Canada had had any genuine opportunity to improve that legislation, we would not have the same problems we have now. In my area alone unemployment has gone up some four times since the NEP. Investment is down, bankruptcies are up, and dreams have simply been destroyed. So the bottom line, Mr. Speaker, is that once again we have some legislation very important to western Canada before this House of Commons, and once again the Government is bringing in closure. Once again we as western Canadians are asking why. What is the purpose? What is the Government doing? It is no wonder the Liberals have no elected representatives in our area; if they keep going at the present rate, they are not going to have any in the future.

Mr. Speaker, one of the things the Government is pushing down our throats which bothers me more than anything else is the fact that it has denied a bargain, one could almost say a constitutional bargain. It is revoking that bargain unilaterally. I am surprised that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), who is a distinguished political historian, does not recognize more fully that this country was based on a series of understandings between the French and English, between central Canada and the eastern part of the country, and between central Canada and the West, the Prairies and British Columbia. Now, from time to time in our history these understandings have been broken. Certainly they are modified from time to time because that is the nature of social progress. One cannot always stick exactly to the original understanding because society changes and understandings have to change with it.
Nevertheless, in the case before us there is a fundamental understanding which is, I think as far as any Canadian is concerned, still relevant and important. The understanding was that while the CPR would be provided with a great number of enormous incentives, and they have all been discussed many times in this debate, they in turn would have certain obligations. In return for all the incentives of land, mineral rights and other things, they have the obligation to see that the Crowsnest Pass rate is maintained.

A related set of understandings, equally relevant today- and in a sense it goes back to Macdonald's national policy- were that encouragement was given the manufacturing sector in central Canada in order to survive. At that time the encouragement thought necessary was a protective tariff, thereby requiring western Canadians to buy their goods at a much higher cost than they would have if they simply went across the border. Western Canadians on the other hand, in return for giving up the cheaper manufactured goods, would themselves be supported in such matters as freight rates. Then we in western Canada, particularly prairie Canada-and we are mostly speaking of wheat-could get our produce on to world markets at a competitive and fair price.
Those understandings are really built very deeply into our society, even if they are not constitutionally embraced. That is what the Bill is destroying. It is destroying these understandings. It would have been one matter if the Bill had done something really creative in connection with the coal lands. It would seem to me that the federal Government and all Canadian Governments have, for far too long, assumed a right to the coal lands. I am now speaking in particular of those in British Columbia. It would have been an act of real understanding had the Government proposed restoring the coal lands to the Province of British Columbia in a separate Bill, as we have suggested.
The whole matter should have been divided into separate Bills. Not only has the Government, in the Bill, gone back on early agreements, bargains and understandings among Canadians in the West and the central part of the country as between the CPR and the farmers, but it has not even tried to restore to the Province of British Columbia what would seem to many of us to be a logical and very valuable ownership right.
The second important point, one which has perhaps not been emphasized sufficiently, is that contrary to what the Government seems to think, namely that the legislation will somehow enhance the activities of Canadian ports, if the Bill does pass the actual result will be that Canadian grain will be diverted, down the line, through U.S. ports. I would be grateful if people who are more knowledgeable with respect to transportation than I would correct me if I am wrong. However, if we do not have the Crow rate, it will be substantially cheaper to export our grain through U.S. ports rather than Canadian ports.
CN and CP already have lines to Duluth, Minnesota where grain could be loaded on to boats for shipment on the Great Lakes. CP owns tracks through its subsidiary Sault Lines to Minneapolis, Minnesota where grain could be loaded on to barges for shipment to export elevators at New Orleans. Minneapolis, as we know, is closer to southern Saskatchewan than Thunder Bay. Because the U.S. inland waterway system is heavily subsidized, barge rates from Minneapolis to New Orleans are less expensive than Lake transportation from Thunder Bay to Montreal.
Under the Government's plan, by 1986 it will cost $8 a tonne less to ship grain rail-barge via New Orleans than rail-Lake via Thunder bay and Montreal. The people who have been studying this matter say that this advantage to New Orleans will grow in succeeding years and it will eventually also become less expensive to ship all rail from Saskatchewan to new Orleans than rail-Lake via Thunder Bay and Montreal. Far from enhancing the role and the activities of Canadian ports, far from helping to make them more prosperous, the long-term consequences of the Government's cancelling of the Crow rate will be to make Canadian ports less prosperous.
A final point about which I am particularly concerned is that in revoking the Crow rate the Government is showing, in the most outspoken fashion possible, that it is really only interested in the big guys, the powerful, the agri-business kind of operation, not the family farm. It is interested in the big corporations, such as the CPR, which has grown into the largest corporate entity in Canada with $16 billion in assets and enormous monopolistic powers. The Government favours more, just as the Tories favour more, the big power, the big corporate entity, the huge cattle rancher, not the average one. The average one has a heard of less than 50. However, the Government is deliberately making life harder for the small and medium-sized farmer or cattleman and making life much easier, in fact making life extremely attractive, I understand, from all evidence that has been put before me, for the big guys, the ones in agri-business and the ones who have huge herds.
It bothers me to find that when other Parties in the country should be concerned with conserving values which we all hold dear, one of them being, of course, the value of independent farmers, they are taking steps which will destroy the independent farmer in this country, ending up by giving support only to huge corporate entities both in the industrial and agricultural sectors.
I would not simply or not only urge that there be amendments, but I would also particularly urge the Official Opposition to join us in opposing the Bill in its entirety.

I would like to talk about the problems of transportation in this country. These problems go back some considerable length of time. I believe it is usually part of the Liberal Party's disposition to choose a Minister who does not like transportation and make him Minister of Transport.
When I first came here the Hon. Jean Marchand, now the distinguished Speaker in the other place, was the Minister of Transport.
