The Government has devised some of the most incompetent methods of dealing with these difficult times in which it finds itself. They have so mismanaged a series of bills for which there was hope of passage that the Opposition becomes enraged at the introduction of each Bill. There are incidents of preliminary discussions of the Bill in press releases and interviews with Ministers who say what the Bill will likely accomplish. 1 can think of several of these occurrences recently. 1 believe it is indicative of the disintegration of the Government that is occurring.
We can think of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) bringing in a Bill on the security force. This country is ready to have a civilian security force because the McDonald Commission pointed out what was wrong. The Government introduced this security force legislation while adding on a few regulations to make it anathema to everyone in the House, including Members on the Government side, I presume. That is why we see difficult legislation such as this, which need not be nearly so difficult, being jammed in at the end of June in an attempt to get it through. We have our extended hours and these rancorous debates and attempts by the Opposition to stop the Government the only way they know how-by prolonging the passage of Bills through the House. The same situation is true of Canagrex. There is nothing the Government could have done to enrage the Opposition more than bring in legislation such as Canagrex and try to pass it in the closing days of the session.
The VIA Rail cutback is another example of Government mismanagement. Of course, VIA Rail was brought in to take over the passenger service of the railway.

How is that relevant?

June 22, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act

I think this has quite a bit to do with the Bill. The CPR and the CNR wanted to get out of the passenger business because they were losing money on moving grain in western Canada. I think they are connected. When the Government implemented VIA Rail-which was a great pleasure to the Party on my left, I am sure-there was a great and sudden cut in services which occurred in the most outrageous and arbitrary fashion imaginable. Of course, as happens whenever the Government takes anything over, it immediately began losing money and becoming more out of control. Yesterday's report on VIA Rail shows that federal subsidies totalled $449 million in 1982, which is up from $422 million in 1981.
It was interesting to hear the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) say in his remarks that the CPR should be brought under public ownership. They want to nationalize it right away because it is making money. They want to turn it into a loser the same as all other Crown corporations. This would be the same philosophy as those who said we should get into the aircraft industry. While the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) pretends that nobody would take over Canadair in 1976 or 1977, the truth of the matter is that the Government paid $47 million for a company for which no one else would pay anything.
At that time the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) accused me of calling the Government stupid for getting into the Canadair deal. I clearly remember a point of order which was raised on that matter. I claimed that 1 had not said that the Government was stupid but that it was simply soft-headed to get into that deal. Some $2 billion later, I think the Minister would probably agree with me. Of course, he no longer has the responsibility for it since he has changed portfolios.
The worst example of all is the Crowsnest Pass rate. This subsidy must be to western Canada what several types of subsidies are to other parts of Canada. That is, they are regional subsidies. For example, we have the salmon enhancement program on the West Coast which probably exists on the East Coast as well. Fisheries do not always operate as profitmaking organizations so the Government puts in money to subsidize them. In other parts of the country there are subsidies for the construction of dams for power. We have the well known protective freight rates that protect central Canada so it will remain the industrial heart of the country.
Up until now the prairie farmer had the Crowsnest Pass freight rate. That was his subsidy. We know that the Government has no Members in that area who have any idea of the enormity of the problem that they are creating. It decided that since those people had not voted Liberal it would retaliate, and that is the purpose of this Bill, to remove the subsidy from the farmer and give it to the CPR.
I can hardly believe my ears when 1 hear the NDP say that they are in favour of the CPR receiving the subsidy rather than the grain producers. But then, what can one expect from that Party? They voted the wrong way on the Constitution. Their leader voted one way and the western membership voted the other way. That is probably their difficulty, having a western membership and a leadership and boardrooms in
Oshawa from where the Party is essentially run. That creates some problems. They had their palace revolt and I presume there will be another one later today.
In any event, the NDP went from the constitutional disaster to the National Energy Program which, in itself, is one of the most disastrous things that ever happened to industry until the Government got into Canadair. Canadair and the National Energy Program are now running neck in neck as to which will be the most damaging blow to the Canadian economy. From there they moved on to the point where approximately one year ago the NDP were the only Party in the House that voted against a Bill which would have cut MPs' pay by 5 per cent and did so over their objections.
From there they moved on to the freedom of information Bill for which everyone in the country has waited many years. They voted against that legislation. The NDP has problems. The 16 per cent of the popular wish which they have in the country has not grown in the ten years that I have been here. They are due for a rather precipitous shrinking in the next election.
I would like to talk about one matter in which British Columbians are interested. I am referring to the provision in the Bill to allow the Government to take back the coal lands from CPR. The coal lands were donated on a two-way switch by the Province of British Columbia. They were given to the CPR but the federal Government was to be the intermediary. Apparently, according to the records which I saw, the Province gave the coal lands to the federal Government and the federal Government, in turn, gave them to the CPR so that it would build the railroad through the mountains. Now the Government will take them back as part of this deal, but it will not return them to the people of British Columbia.
These are among the richest coal lands remaining in Canada. They have an almost unlimited amount of very superior quality coal. Once again the federal Government will get its hands on them. Whenever it sees anything that can be sold at a profit or into which it can become involved to prevent a profit-
Order, please. I regret to interrupt the Hon. Member but his allotted time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak once again on the Crow rate issue and to avail the House of Commons of my deep and great knowledge and understanding of this subject, a knowledge and understanding surpassed only by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Flis) who hails from downtown Toronto.
We must remember that this afternoon we are really talking about the motion put before the House by the Hon. Member for Rosemont (Mr. Lachance), the intention of which is again to limit debate on this subject. It is certainly my intention and
June 22, 1983

it is the intention of Members on this side of the House to vote in opposition to the motion, which is tantamount to closure.
The point at issue is that second reading debate deals with the principle of the Bill before us. If second reading is passed and the matter goes to committee, it is assumed that there is general agreement on the principles in the Bill. It is then put forward to committee so taht the details can be examined. We all know after having listened to the rather limited debate so far that there is no general agreement on the principles of this Bill. There are several principles on which there is no real agreement, and debate should continue until some form of consensus has been worked out.
The Hon. Member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski) spoke eloquently this morning. He gave rise to suspicions which I am sure secretly exist with all Hon. Members, suspicions of a conspiracy between the Liberals opposite and the New Democratic Party to my left. Just listening to these two sets of gentlemen, it might not come immediately to mind that that is exactly what is taking place, but let us examine the strategies employed by these two like-minded political Parties.
First I will take the Liberals as an example. They have presented us with a wall of silence. They know that their position is indefensible and for that reason they have not cared to try to defend it. The minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), who should have the interests of farmers at heart, has spoken only once during the debate. His sole contribution was to give notice of time allocation; that is all the Minister of Agriculture has done.
We have listened for the last two days and I do not think there have been more than tow Members of the Liberal Party who cared to stand up and present us with any views at all. We heard the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Gourde) speak very briefly for about two or three minutes this morning. His sole contribution was a diatribe against Mr. Brian Mulroney who will shortly be the Right Hon. Brian Mulroney.
Hear, hear!

It was evident that he was scared of what this gentleman might do. He might well be scared because his job as the Hon. Member for Levis is at stake and he knows it full well, as do other Liberal Members from Quebec.
Now I go to the Members of the New Democratic Party. I thought for a while that they too were engaging in this conspiracy of silence. This morning while this matter was under debate they did not put up a single speaker, and I think they have only put up two speakers so far this afternoon. If we examine their approach to the matter, we will see that it has been one of mindless opposition-there is to be absolutely no change to the Crow rates and the system of agriculture in western Canada which has existed since the last century, a century where they still belong. Their contribution has been described by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) as reactionary. I would describe it as blockheadedness. They want no change at all. They want little elevators every four miles along the railway track. They want farmers going along on horses and carts delivering a few bushels of grain. They want the old
Western Grain Transportation Act
boxcars. They are not prepared to look at new modifications to the western transportation system. They belong back in the days of the horse and buggy.
When we examine the approach taken by the Liberal Government and the New Democratic Party, we see that it is a conspiracy because Members of the NDP know they are not rational and responsible and will not take a look at what the western grain transportation system really needs. They know full well that they will fail, that there is no way we will return to the days of the horse and buggy. They will go back to their constituencies and say "We fought against the Crow", while in actual fact they played into the hands of their colleagues in the Liberal Government and did more than anyone else to ensure that the Crow proposal in its present form goes through.
We, on the other hand, have taken what I would describe to be a reasonable, rational and responsible approach to the problem. We recognize the need for change. We want to see a modern and efficient grain transportation system. To that end, our transportation critic, the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), has very eloquently presented a series of principles which we would like to see incorporated in any Bill that deals with Crow rates.
First we have to realize that this is a very imperfect world and that every major grain exporting country engages in some form of subsidization to its grain producers, one way or another. Therefore, we need a freight rate for western grain which will enable our producers to be competitive with producers in the United States, Argentina, Australia and other countries. We agree that there should be a special rate for the shipment of grains.
Second, we believe in the principle of providing fair compensation to the railways. We know that the accountants who work for the railways have some pretty sharp pencils; they can do wonders with figures. But there is no doubt at the present time that the recompense of the railways is not sufficient for them to engage in major capital improvements.
Third, we want to guarantee producers an efficient, cost-effective and reliable grain transportation system.
We agree, as a fourth principle, that the present distortions which exist in the marketplace for transportation should be removed. There are natural advantages to doing certain things in certain parts of Canada. Grain can be grown better in the West than it can in the Maritimes; livestock can be produced in some areas better than in others. We need a system which maintains the natural advantages of doing certain things in certain areas of the country. To do that will render the whole system most efficient and will result in a natural and efficient allocation of resources.
The farmers want a freight rate that is known and predictable, not like the one in the Bill where no one knows what the rate will be years hence. Farmers must know where they will stand a year or two from now.

June 22, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act 1 could go on at great length on this most important matter but I see that my time has come to an end. In conclusion, I and the other Members of this Party will vote in opposition to the proposition put forward by the Hon. Member for Rosemont.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Pepin that Bill C-155, an Act to facilitate the transportation, shipping and handling of western grain and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport; and the motion of Mr. Lachance (p. 26521).

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak against Bill C-155, and rightly so. Having been raised on a farm, 1 want to say that the Crow is really outdated and needs overhaul. It should have been done years ago. However, the Government has not addressed the problem.
The Gilson Commission came out with a reasonable report. It would have been acceptable. However, the Government has decided instead to railroad this Bill through. It will divide the East from the West even more than it is today. It will destroy the hopes of Canadians and the unity of this country.
Having been raised on a farm, I quite appreciate this situation with regard to grain handling, cattle raising or hog raising. Grain handling certainly does not meet the needs of
today. 1 remember the time when we used a team of horses to haul 60 bushels of grain. At times we used four horses and hauled 80 bushels. The elevators are still the same today; they do not meet our present needs.
This Government has destroyed hope and incentive in this country. With regard to grain transportation, we are still in the horse and buggy days; there is no question about that. It really bothers me. Because our transportation system is so outdated, we are losing between $1.5 billion and $2 billion in sales. This proposed Bill will make the situation even worse. This Government, which is further dividing Canadians, is now beginning to crumble. Thank God it is coming to an end.
There are only four supporters left.
The Liberals are so interested in this Bill that we now have only four Members of that Party in the Chamber.
Not one from western Canada.
That is true. The Government is not doing what is best for the country but what is best for the Party. It is unfortunate that it has reached this stage.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: It is best for Canada.

It certainly is not. The grain handling system does not meet the needs of today. This not only affects the grain and hog producer but it is affecting the coal, sulphur, lumber and packing industries. They are being destroyed. Thousands and thousands of jobs have been lost in the last several years from Vancouver to Toronto. It is needless to say how many packing plants have been closed in western Canada because of inadequate transportation and the Crow rate. There is no question in my mind about that.
At one time I was an employee of Canada Packers in Winnipeg. That was during the hungry thirties or, as some refer to it, the good old days. I and a couple of other fellows were going to Toronto to look for a job. In Winnipeg we met a bunch of guys who were returning from Toronto. They told us that they had been there and there was no sense in our going. Therefore, a couple of us decided to go to Canada Packers for a job. When we arrived, there were about 300 people waiting to be called for a job. Lo and behold, on the third day the guy called me, accepted me and gave me a job.
It is tough working in the packing industry, but very interesting. It is a shame what the Government has done to the packing industry of western Canada at the expense of the taxpayers. It has not only done this to the packing industry, but to the transportation industry and the economy in general. How does the Government expect to implement this Bill in its present form when most Canadians object to it? In spite of that, the Minister is determined to railroad the Bill through against the will of Canadian taxpayers and the industry.
When the Gilson Report was commissioned by the Government, there were consultations between the industry and the farmers in order to arrive at an acceptable rate or an acceptable proposal to be made by the Government. The Government
June 22, 1983

ignored the proposal and has come up with a Bill that is definitely unacceptable to western Canadians and Canadians in general.

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a point of order. I want to direct your Honour's attention to the fact that over and over in the course of the debate today there has been reference to an undertaking made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) that, in the event this matter passes second reading, there will be an opportunity for the Standing Committee seized with the responsibility of this legislation to travel across this country in order to hear representations from a variety of people who are interested in the legislation.
The point of order I raise, Mr. Speaker, is that 1 do not believe this to be a statement that was actually made by the Minister. As 1 understand it, there was no commitment made. I raise this point of ordr as the Minister is now in the House, so that we may have this information clearly and unequivocally before us before taking a vote on second reading.
My point is that I do not believe that representations should be made which are not based on fact and which in fact would mislead Members of the House of Commons. This should be clearly stated by the Minister, and I would appreciate it if he could address himself to the question of whether or not he is agreeable to having the committee travel the country to hear representations made by interested parties, particularly those in western Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: In the interests of moving the business of the House forward, I will accept the Hon. Member's point although as he knows, it is not a point of order. However, if the Hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) wishes to reply, I will consider it part of the business of the House.
Mr. Speaker, in only one minute I can put that to rest. I made no such commitment.
It was on the news yesterday.

Yes, but that was not a quote from the Minister of Transport; it was an interpretation made by the reporter. I made no such commitment because I am not allowed to make such a commitment. I am told by my House Leader that this decision is to be made first by the committee.
Are you receptive to that suggestion?

If the committee wants to travel, it must ask the permission of the House and the House may or may not give that permission. I am not willing to anticipate what view the committee would have on that subject.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure I will not add anything to this debate that has not been said already, but I feel that it is appropriate for me, as a grandson on one side and a great grandson and the other of pioneers who
Western Grain Transportation Act came to western Canada during the Sifton era and settled on 160 acres of land and attempted to produce grain, to say a few words on this debate.
I do not need to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that most of these pioneers who came to western Canada and bought 160 acres of land for $20 subsequently sold that land at very highly escalated prices. Not for one minute would anyone suggest that capital gains made on that land should revert back to the Government or anybody else. All of those families held the assets that they were given as pioneers. Therefore, I always have some difficulty when reference is made to the notion that the shareholders of CPR who also got some land should indeed turn that land back over to the Government. 1 say that in fairness to the events of that particular era.
I do want to say, Mr. Speaker, that the farmer is the servant of all and the master of none. Yet he produces the most vital commodity to man, food. This Bill massively interferes with the process of growing, producing and shipping food in western Canada. That process of growing, producing and shipping food is an evolutionary process in the West. It occurs over a considerable length of time, not over short periods of time. When any Government tries to change the process of this evolution, it had better be mighty careful that it does not move too fast and create revolutionary change rather than evolutionary change. The system can be partially destroyed by revolutionary change in this most vital of areas, the growth of food.
What do 1 have to say, Mr. Speaker, about the rate of change and the manner of change that is being made to the food growing industry in western Canada by Bill C-155? First, I want to say that Bill C-155, in my view, is massively flawed. It is an administrative and regulatory nightmare. I say that as a former Minister in the Province of Alberta who had the opportunity for seven years to structure and administer regulations.
This is a depressing Bill. Indeed, as I said earlier in the House, there are 40,278 lawyers in Canada, more per capita, I think, than in any other free country in the world. It is my belief that this Bill, as I read it, would create the need for several thousand more lawyers. It is not specific. The wording itself is, in most instances, unbelievably vague.
Second, Mr. Speaker, the rate of change to the freight rate structure is, in my view, much too rapid, even though the Minister has brought forth the ceiling which I appreciate very much and which would tend to help slow the process down. I wish that that ceiling had been incorporated earlier so that many of the adverse aspects of it could have been ruled out earlier.
Increasing input costs on any commodity by ten times in the next decade would create a change that is just too rapid. I am not particularly against changing the Crow, and 1 have put a motion on the paper that proposes indexing the Crow to inflation because I realize that it must change.

It would be higher.

June 22, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act

No, no. With a ceiling, the rate of change would be slower than the change proposed by the Minister. It is the rate of change that bothers me. It is much too rapid a change over too short a period of time. It is revolutionary change. It would destroy a large part of the western economic industry that I grew up with, those little farmers who are dependent upon an income which is quite limited.
The third point that I draw to the attention of the Minister, Mr. Speaker, is that the redistribution of the Crow subsidy is, in my view, not equitable. It simply must be more related to what Gilson said and must be examined in much more depth in terms of the manner in which that money is redistributed. I know a suggestion has been made about freedom of choice, but I have some difficulty with that suggestion also. I am bothered by the fact that indeed, because of this suggestion, land speculators would tend to buy land for the simple purpose of harvesting the Crow. The Crow as I calculate it may indeed be in the order of $20 to $25 an acre, depending on whether it was calculated on an acreage basis over the entire period of the increase in freight rates. That is quite a bit of money per acre.
I can see land speculators going for this in a substantive way which would increase the price of land substantially. They would rent the land using some form of contract and pocket the entire Crow subsidy.
It balances out.

There may be a balance, but I do not know that there is. I simply suggest that the freedom of choice proposition, through it is appealing and contains some aspects which I find acceptable, would have to be studied further.
Sooner or later you have to make up your mind. To govern is to choose. You have to choose.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to indicate to the Minister the fourth reason that I have difficulty with the Bill, and I agree with the Minister when he says that sooner or later a choice must be made. I quite agree that at some point a choice must be made. I thought I had just barely started, Mr. Speaker. These nine minutes have gone by quickly.
The fourth problem with the Bill, of course, is that it increases considerably the disparity between raw and finished food products in the West. I do not think that that is appropriate for the West at all.
The fifth problem I have, of course, is that the politics surrounding the issue are just terrible. The entire political scene of Canada is not the appropriate forum in which to change the very fundamental basis upon which the West opened up and upon which indeed it grew. I suggest to the Minister that if he were to serve another term, and I am not wishing that on him, he might delay this measure for another four or five years and in fact bring it back in four or five years.
When the Bill goes to committee I hope the Minister will do everything possible to ensure that the Committee travels. I know he cannot say that it should but he could certainly
suggest that. The Committee should hold hearings in Regina and some of the small towns in the West and I know the Minister could arrange that if he wanted to.
For how many years?

Mr. Speaker, in the West there are three land transportation systems. The first is the railway system, the second is the pipeline system and the third is the highway system. We built a massive highway system under total subsidization by two forms of Government. Governments own the land base and do the maintenance. There is not a toll station on any highway in the West. That massive subsidy given to the highway system has literally destroyed the railway system in the West. I have no difficulty with the federal Government and some provincial Governments massively subsidizing the rebuilding of the railway system because they have done so for the competitive highway system. No truck pays one cent for the use of the highway system in the West, except for the very modest licence fee.
There is no subsidy for the pipeline system either. I investigated the question of shipping grain by pipeline and when I was a Minister in Alberta I also investigated the question of shipping coal by pipeline. Pipeline shipping for some food commodities will eventually find its place in western Canada.
The railway system has been neglected, however. It has suffered inflationary pressures. The solution to its problems has been delayed for years and, as a result, inflation has caused distortion. The Minister is trying to correct the problems too quickly. He is trying to impose revolutionary change on a system which cannot and should not take it.
I do not disagree with the work the Minister has done on this issue in the past but I believe it is incomplete. Hearings should be held in the West so that people can appear before the Committee and have their say.
Mr. Speaker, I have a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
That is twice in two days. The Hon. Member for Vegreville is quite correct. As far as I recall, the Minister of Transport has not spoken on the previous question. In any event, 1 do not think we ought to entertain an invitation to make speeches in the way it has been done. If the Minister of Transport wishes to speak he can be recognized.
I indicated to another Hon. Member earlier that I would accept a point of order for the purpose of allowing the business of the House to go forward.

Mr. Speaker, I will not make a speech but just a couple of remarks.
I was asked if 1 was going to recommend to the Committee that it should travel. I indicated to the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) a few minutes ago what my House Leader had told me a couple of times, that the decision to travel or not to travel is for the Committee to make. I do not know why CBC quoted me the way it did yesterday-
Is there a deal or is there not?

No, there is no deal at all. If there is a deal, it is public and that is what I am talking about now. There is no agreement secretly arrived at. I said that the Committee must express its views first on whether it will travel or not. It has then to make a request to the House and the House has to approve or disapprove. I have no intention of questioning that pattern.
Western Grain Transportation Act
On the question whether I will make a speech before the end of the debate, this is the first time I have been asked to do that.
I made a fairly long speech at the beginning of the debate and I thought that I had exhausted most of the subject.
At the first meeting of the Committee I intend to review everything and to try and answer all questions on the 10 per cent, the 31.1 million tonnes and all that.
The Hon. Member for Vegreville follows me very carefully and I follow him very carefully so he knows that I have expressed my views on most of these issues. When I have wanted to I have done so. In answer to a question from his colleague on the 31.1, I remember sending a little note to my friend to the effect that he must have observed that I had answered that question.
On the 10 per cent question, which is the difference between the cost of rail transportation and the transportation of grain at the international price of grain, I have said this is the figure we have arrived at. We started higher than that. I can defend the 10 per cent very well both in statistical terms and intellectual terms, but I have said that I would be willing to listen to argument.
I do not think I have much to add at this point. I will be available in Committee and I will do my very best to answer all questions and inquiries. Some of my friends seem to accuse me-I am making a speech now, Mr. Speaker and I do not want to do that.
When will the Committee hearings start?

We will start as soon as we can. If the Bill is passed today I expect the steering committee will meet tomorrow. Perhaps that question should be addressed to the chairman. We will get organized as rapidly as we can and start with energy next week. We will do our best to lay the foundation for the rest of the work and make a study and analysis of the different parts of the debate. I will be delighted to prove to the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) that every part is interrelated essentially, and not only in passing. We will do all the work and then we will continue.

Mr. Speaker, we may be facilitating the debate and I appreciate your indulgence.
Perhaps I could direct a question to the chairman of the Standing Committee on Transport and ask whether he has any views on when the Committee hearing might commence. Also, will arrangements be made for travel or will he await the decision of the steering committee?

Mr. Speaker, I have some pretty definite views but, as the Hon. Member knows, in my role as chairman I have tried to be the servant and not the master of the Committee. As soon as the Bill is referred to the Committee I intend to call a meeting of the subcommittee on procedure and agenda. I will have a proposal
26688

June 22, 1983

to put before the subcommittee at the time. We will discuss it there and bring it before the full Committee, hopefully before the end of June. Included in that proposal I will have a suggestion for the Committee to consider with regard to our schedule of hearings.
Whether we travel or not is a matter, as the Minister has rightly said, in my opinion, for the committee to make. However, I remind the Hon. Member that unless we have authority from the House, we cannot travel. Also, unless we have authority from the House we cannot engage professional or expert staff. Therefore, our decision will be somewhat limited by the reference we receive from the House.

speechtext: The Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) on a point of order.

Mr. Speaker, if, as and when the Transport Committee, or its steering committee, requests the House for an order of reference to travel from place to place in Canada, to hear witnesses and to be provided with staff, may I ask the Minister if he will use his good offices to support such a request? Mr. Speaker, 1 must at the outset say that I am puzzled and a little distressed by the answer which the Minister has given. I want to make it clear that never was there any deal struck between the Minister and myself or myself and anyone else in regard to how the Bill would be handled. However, I will mull that over in the next nine minutes.
I want to make it clear, Mr. Speaker, that when this Bill was introduced in those days immediately prior to May 9, we already had an inkling of what was to be contained in the Bill. We were aware that the Government was intent on changing the Crowsnest Pass freight rates. We believed then that the change being proposed was a change which would work to the detriment of those who would have to pay the bills, and not only to the detriment of the farming community but to the detriment of the country as a whole. On May 10 we made that opposition known by voting against the Bill at first reading.
We still hold true to that position, that what the Government is proposing to do by way of change to the Crow rate will do nothing but harm to the farming community of western Canada, particularly on the Prairies. It will do nothing but harm to the economy of Canada with regard to our potential for exporting the grain which we grow here. We used this as the economic base for a very large part of our country. It has in fact made this country famous all around the world. I do not have to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the competitive position of the grain farmers of western Canada will be detrimentally affected by the proposals the Minister has brought forward. There is no one in the world who can possibly believe that if you add to the price of a commodity in the world market it will somehow enhance your competitive position.
Our major competitors are heavily subsidized. In some instances they are granted absolutely free movement of grain from the farm to the point of distribution. Our American competitors are given a substantial subsidy through the use of
Western Grain Transportation Act
the waterways to get their grain to market. Our Australian competitors are much closer to the shipping ports and do not have to carry the extremely high cost of transportation. Given all that, no right minded individual could believe that to alter the Crowsnest Pass freight rate and place an additional burden on Canadian farmers would in any way improve their capacity to sell their product to those who must buy it.
There are compensatory factors.

Having said that, if the Government is now telling us, as it is, that it will begin a process of compensation which will ultimately become larger than the subsidy we now carry, then I suggest that is foolish. To add an administrative cost on top of all the other changes in order to bring the farmer back to where he was before, competitively speaking, surely must not make any sense to any objective observer.
Again, Mr. Speaker, what the Government is doing is wrong. The Crowsnest Pass freight rate is a subsidy, paid for in great part by the public of Canada. When properly used, it gives our grain farmers a competitive edge in world markets. For us to turn around and start tinkering with it over any number of years can only work a hardship. Therefore, the Government has taken a very regressive and regrettable step.
The Conservative Members are aware right from the very beginning that we said the Bill was complex. There were three parts to it and it should be proceeded with separately. The upgrading of the railroads should be viewed separately since it deals not only with the transportation of grain but with the transportation of all commodities from coast to coast. We also made it clear that we thought that the disposition of the Dominion coal lands was a separate matter without any relationship to the Crowsnest Pass freight rate and should be dealt with in a separate way. Finally, we suggested that if the Government was to go ahead with its proposed changes, then they should be dealt with for what they really are, an attempt by the Government to alter dramatically the arrangement entered into so many years ago from which the CPR and others have derived significant benefits.
Over the years Canada has been extremely competitive in its ability to move and sell its grain. We should view that matter separately. I appreciate very much the fact that the Conservatives supported our position on that, but unfortunately we failed in that to this point. The battle is not yet over, it is just over for now. We still believe those principles should be divided, we still believe the matter should be dealt with in that way.
The Minister seems to feel that somehow or other the farmers of Canada are not going to be as detrimentally affected as we believe they are and as I think some on the Conservative benches believe they are. I have had letters from farmers from all across the Prairies who are bringing to my attention and the attention of others the dilemma which will confront them. I will read one sent from Birch Hills to one of my colleagues. It said:
We have gone back into our income tax files and have some figures for you-

In 1973, from a gross income of $63,500, their net income was $25,400. By 1978 they had a gross income of $107,400 and a net income of $22,500. Note the decrease. By 1982 they had a gross income of $130,000, and a net income of $16,000. It is the additional costs heaped on the farming community, whether it be for fuel, fertilizer or replacement of machinery, whether it be through taxes, which has eaten away all of the surplus which should have been there to provide for that family's welfare. The letter then goes on to say:
We took our production of 1982 and if Pepin gets his way and we pay 75 cents per bushel freight by 1990, we would have to pay $30,000 in freight as we produced approximately 40,000 bushels of grain in 1982.
We have never had a $30,000 net profit in any year since we started farming some 27 years ago.
Wrong, wrong, wrong, again!

No one can say it more eloquently than that. The fact of the matter is, Mr. Minister, that the farmers affected by this increase in costs cannot afford it. I do not know how better to say it. If someone cannot afford what you are attempting to foist upon them, they will go out of business, Sir. When they go out of business they will not be replaced by anyone else and we will have lost for all time that agricultural capacity, that revenue, which we have derived over the years from the sale of their products. We will never be able to recover it.
You are taking one-

I am taking that farmer as representative of many farmers. If you give me the time, I will read the rest. I am putting on the record one letter taken from a number of letters, which is representative of what we understand to be the situation of the farmers in western Canada.
I will close by saying that it is obvious that ten minutes does not allow me an opportunity to put on the record how strongly we feel about what is being proposed. I am disturbed by the Minister's suggestion that the hearing process may be forestalled or foreshortened. I am concerned that the Government may attempt to push this through over the objections of farmers like this one. He and his family deserve to be heard but they cannot be heard if the hearings are in Ottawa. Obviously they cannot afford to make the trip.
Therefore, I urge that the Government pay particular heed to the people who will be most affected. It is not their representatives we want to hear at this point; we have heard from them. We know the decisions of the institutional representatives. Who we have to hear from now are the people who pay the bills.
We oppose what this Government is doing and, by God, we will oppose it to the bitter end. We will oppose it in December of this year, we will oppose it into next year if this Government does not pay attention to these people.

Mr. Speaker, we are here to debate the issue of whether or not the question should be put. The answer is very simple, of course. It is that I am not "prepared up with that to put", because I like to go back to the first principle. Oftentimes, if one goes back to
the first principles, one finds different answers from what one would otherwise. We all recognize that what is required, needed and must happen is a total upgrading of the railway system of western Canada, including that of British Columbia. I have been lobbied heavily by many interests in British Columbia saying, "Vote for the Bill because we must have the railways upgraded". I would agree that the railways must be upgraded. However, they do not seem to understand that to do it this way is raping western Canadian farmers. It is not in the best interests of British Columbia that the Prairies be raped in this particular manner.
I am a Prairie boy and they say that one can take the boy out of the Prairie but not the Prairie out of the boy.
I think of western Canada, Gladstone and Morris, Virden, Eyebrow, Elbow, Belle Plaine, Carstairs and Olds, right across the Prairies, those little beacons of light bringing civilization at night, right across the vast plains, and of the many people in them. I understand how they feel about this kind of thing taking place because I can tell Hon. Members how many of the people in that part of the world are thinking about this right now. They have known the CPR for a long time. They found that CPR, rather than being a good neighbour, has been a exploiter over the years. What may not be known in the House is that starting back in the 1950s, the CPR reached a corporate decision which it has been carrying out ever since.
Anyone on the Prairies looking about with the native suspicion we all have, has realized what happened. First, the CPR owned houses in practically every division for its executives. It sold them off and the money was drained out of the railway. There was a formation of Canadian Pacific oil and gas. Guess what? There was the draining off into a separate company of all the mineral wealth that it had been given. There is nothing wrong with either one of those two things, if its basic contract with the prairie settler were to be kept. Unfortunately, it has not.
One could consider Marathon Realty and the vast real estate holdings in many cities of the West which, again, were bled off by the railway. One can consider what the railways have done in terms of deterioration of passenger service. Who would want to ride their ruddy trains by the time they were done actually allowing them to go totally downhill? As a result, they got rid of that, and the Government took it over and formed VIA Rail. The only thing worse than VIA Rail, I have found in North America, happens to be Amtrak, and the American railways did the same.
Over a 20 years period, why has the Government not taken a look at the original contracts and perhaps even social contracts with the people of western Canada? Why has it not been able to realize that the CPR was almost deliberately allowing those rail lines to become obsolete, allowing the whole matter to settle down? It had taken the profits, moved them over to Canadian Pacific Investments. It had taken the profits and
June 22, 1983

26691 moved them here. It had taken most of the profitable aspects of the railway and moved so that, quite frankly, I doubt if the CPR would care at all if the Government wished to nationalize the rail line. It received its money and it moved it, rather than living up to its responsibilities to western Canada.
What have a succession of federal Governments done about this situation? I have not heard much talk over the years, saying, "Hey, wait a minute now. Is the CPR really entitled not to build more grain cars, because we are short of grain cars, in view of its initial contracts and its initial gifts from the people of Canada?" We do not see Government of Canada grain cars. We see Province of Alberta grain cars, grain hoppers. These should all be made by the CPR, paid for by the CPR and operated by the CPR. If it is at a loss, let us consider where the profits went. They went into other areas of the company having nothing to do with the railway.
The prairie farmer is entitled to have a committee take a very solid look at the actions of this giant of a company, this colossus of profits which has really moved away from the rail lines, and I hope such a committee does study it.
One of the other reasons your prairie lad is suspicious of the railway and of a succession of Liberal Governments, practically since Confederation, is that at one time one could send a widget from Toronto to the West for a dollar. However, if one wanted to send a widget from the West eastward, it cost $2. I will give only one example. Show me a flour mill existing in western Canada today. The reason one does not exist there is because of the freight rate structure of this country which gives real favouritism to the East.
What is taking place now is another rip-off of western Canada. The whole matter disturbs me mightily. Darn it, how long does the Government think the people of the West will put up with central Canada ripping them off in every way? That is exactly what changing the Crow rate will do to us again.
All I can say to the Government is, for heaven's sake, let us take another look at the whole matter. Let us go back to the basic problem of upgrading western rail lines. If we are to pay for it, let us ensure that all the people of Canada pay for it in a proper way, where the Quebecer contributes as much as anyone else, where the Maritimer takes part in it, where Ontario pays its share, rather than doing it in such a way as to lay most of the cost on the back of the prairie farmer.
I warn the Government, the Liberal majority, that if it goes through with this dastardly scheme, it will lay the seeds of discontent in the West all over again. Generations of prairie people will never forget the dastardly deed the Government will carry out with the Bill on top of their backs and at their expense. For heaven's sake, the Government must reconsider. This is no way to run a railway.

Hear, hear!

I rise to enter the debate on Bill C-155, but before making the comments I had intended to make, I would draw the attention of the Chair to the emotions of the last Hon. Member to speak who was trying to represent the concerns and frustrations of western Canadians, which is his job to do in a Party which, of course, represents all of Canada, every territory and every Province. One can see why there are differences of opinion in this Party from time to time, occasioned by the differences which occur in the country as a whole. It was with great sympathy that I listened to my colleague from British Columbia trying to represent these frustrations. I come from Ontario and I wish other eastern or central Canadians could try truly to understand the message being brought to us by our western colleagues.
I consider this matter from the point of view of any business person. When business, which is a large business, runs into the kind of problems being faced by the country today, which can only be described as a massive material handling problem, it considers the various kinds of solutions it might give. It could, of course, raise prices to solve the economic problems of grain handling, or it could squeeze suppliers to farmers. It could say, "Lower the price of your grain and you will be more competitive on the world markets and all the other costs will have to be borne", or it could reduce costs, which any sensible business would try to do. What it would not do would be to attempt to reduce its markets deliberately by letting its product price go up too high to be competitive.
What have we done to attempt to reduce the costs of grain handling in this country rather than just throw the load on to the farmers? Have we really done some serious technological studies on the size of rolling stock, the shape of hopper cars or the kind of handling practices at either end, the filling or emptying of those cars? Have we seriously done a cost study on the electrification of rail lines? Have we performed a serious cost study on the conversion of engines to compressed natural gas, which is in abundance in this country and which would certainly lower the costs of grain handling? Have we considered the efficiencies of the trunk lines and branch lines of the railroads in an effort to make them more cost effective?
In the last election, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) promised that he would doubletrack the railroads. Although he was whistling in the wind, he had the right idea in terms of cost efficiency. To do so, would undoubtedly lower the cost of transportation of grain.
I believe the railways have an obligation to look at these alternatives, such as to improve their signals and do all those things that would make them more cost effective. Another alternative is super mechanization of port facilities to improve the turnaround factor to get the cars to handle grain more quickly.
The Hon. Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) talked a few moments ago about pipeline transportation for grain. That may sound fanciful but it is not. It is quite feasible and should be seriously considered before raising the prices to farmers.

June 22, 1983

There are many things that need to be done to reduce the costs long before we raise the prices. Of course, we should not forget the job creation prospects in all of these technological developments. That would be a real boon to the country today. However, it has become a national psychosis in Canada, a mind-set of business, Government and labour that whenever you have a problem, you should raise the prices and the consumer will pick up the bill.
What incentive will the railroads have to improve their efficiency or service if we simply give them more money and just open the door to price increases forever? How will increased costs of grain caused by both the transportation cost increases and the operating inefficiencies that will result, help Canada's export grain sales and balance of payments? Obviously, the answer is that it will not.
This House is considering the possibility of establishing a standing committee on science and technology. Such a committee could very well look into these problems of grain handling and perform a detailed examination of the possible technological improvements and cost cutting potentials of advanced rail technology. That is something the Government should have done long before bringing in a Bill such as this.
In specifically addressing the question of whether we should immediately put the question to the House which would cut off all further debate and examination, I wish to say that 1 do not think an offhanded treatment of a century-old institution which will perpetuate the inefficiencies while increasing the cost is a proper step. 1 think it is well worth debating. Government Members should be clamouring for greater debate and more solutions and consensus rather than remaining quiet so that the debate will not interfere with the forthcoming summer holidays. Discussion, consensus and agreement is what is required of Parliament, not division and acrimony. Putting the question and muzzling debate is not the way to get to the satisfactory conclusion of this issue.
In the absence of any commitment by the Minister or the Government to let the farmers be heard by a travelling task force which would let them make their concerns known and give their suggestions for solutions would occasion any concerned Member of this House to vote no to the question.

Mr. Speaker, we have had a widespread debate on this Bill with many comments and recommendations for improvement.
1 would like to pay tribute to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) for spending almost the entire time of the debate in the House.
Hear, hear!

It is not often that a Minister does so, and he should be commended.
Having said that, I must say that I am very disappointed that the Minister was not prepared to stand in the House to speak at some length about what has been said by Members on this side of the House so he could give us an idea of what he will be doing when the Bill goes to committee. I was also very
disappointed by the fact that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) came into the debate solely for the purpose of giving notice of closure on this Bill. The Minister of Agriculture should be dedicated to the welfare and well-being of the agricultural community. This is a Bill which affects every aspect of agriculture and, in fact, affects every region of the country from coast to coast. Having spent some $850,000 on advertising the policy of the Government, 1 suppose that Government Members do not feel they have to get into this debate and make their contribution.
The Minister of Transport has the opportunity at this time to rebuild our transportation system and make it one of the most modern and best transportation systems in the world. He has not chosen to do that. Instead, he has chosen to bring in a Bill which is unsatisfactory to the majority of people in this country. This Bill should be withdrawn.
Hear, hear!

It should be withdrawn and a special committee should be set up to study Canada's transportation system at length and to consider the effects of any change in the Crow rate on the western Prairies and on agricultural producers.
There is much concern over this Bill. I have received letters from hundreds of my constituents, not only from farmers but also from those who live in the cities and towns the economy of which is dependent upon agriculture. The farmers are concerned because their product price is down and their input costs are up. At this time they cannot afford any increase in costs. The Hon. Member who spoke a few moments ago indicated that five times the Crow would result in a cost per acre of $25. That assumes that every acre is seeded. If you work on a two-year rotation, the cost of freighting grain would average at about $50 an acre. When this cost is added to the costs of fuel, taxes and other charges, it becomes almost prohibitive.
I receive letters from chambers of commerce and city and town councils expressing concern about what will happen as a result of the increase in freight rates taking money away from their communities. It amounts to hundreds of millions of dollars in losses to the communities. When we talk with farmers, city people or members of corporations, they express concern about the railways. There is a mistrust of the railways, both CN and CP. They know that over the yars the railways have received branch-line subsidies, hopper cars and grants. They ask whether the railways have spent that money wisely. When we talk to farmers in areas where branch-line subsidies were paid to the railways and discover that there has not been a train over the lines for eight or ten years, we understand the concern and the mistrust. Also they ask about the $651 million, the guaranteed annual income which the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) is interested in giving the railways. They ask how accurate that figure of $651 million is. We do not know.

This is what we must know and why distrust exists in the minds of people across the country. As well the committee should investigate the freedom of choice proposition put forward by the Hon. speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, May 27, 1983, consideration of the motion of Mr. Trudeau that Bill C-152, an Act Respecting the Organization of the Government of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1983 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as we have just heard, we are dealing this evening with Bill C-152, a Bill introduced by the Government dealing basically with two items, one being the reorganization of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, as well as that of the Department of External Affairs and the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. The second item the Bill deals with the is the addition of a number of parliamentary secretaries to the new Department which will be created by the passage of the Bill if, indeed, it is passed, expanding jurisdiction to include Senators as well as Members of the House of Commons.
The new Department of Regional and Industrial Expansion will be developed from the former Department of Industry,
Government Organization Act, 1983 Trade and Commerce and the Department of Regional and Economic Expansion. This particular piece of legislation will have a profound impact on various sections of the country, particularly the one for which the original Department of Regional and Economic Expansion was devised back in 1969.
Although I think there is much justification for dealing with the expansion of the bureaucracy to include an additional number of parliamentary secretaries, which no doubt will appease a number of those disgruntled backbenchers on the Opposition benches, nonetheless, I do not believe that time permits me to deal with that particular aspect of the Bill, even though I would much like to do so.
The provisions of the Bill which, as I have mentioned, deals with and would particularly affect the section of the country from which I come, namely, Atlantic Canada, have proceeded as far as departmental changes are concerned, despite the fact that this Parliament has not had the opportunity to deal with or pass any particular phase or aspect of the Bill. The Government has proceeded with changes within the Department; setting up and reorganizing its departmental to accomodate the proposed changes in the Department despite the fact that the elected representatives from the region have not had any opportunity for parliamentary input. Considering the fact that the Bill was only moved for second reading on May 27, it seems the Government is determined to move on with the Bill and the implementation of its provisions despite the fact that Parliament has not had an opportunity for input. This leaves us to be somewhat suspicious, as always, of the motives and the underlying reasons for the Government to move forward with such haste.
I do appreciate this opportunity to take Members of the House and people throughout Canada who might be interested, particularly those in Atlantic Canada, on a brief walk through the history of what DREE was all about and the reason for its implementation back in 1979. DREE was created in 1969 by the present Government. In the words of the Throne Speech at the time, it was established and was to be "charged with objectives of ensuring that all people in all areas and regions of our country have as equal an access as possible to the opportunities of Canada's development''.
What did that mean to the people of Atlantic Canada and eastern Canada, since this was originally designed to include all of those regions of Canada east of Trois Rivieres? The original intention of the program was to reduce disparities between the regions of Canada that had been subjected to particular economic hardships over the years. It had particular reference to eastern and Atlantic Canada.
1 am sure all Members are aware that Atlantic Canada initially played a very important role in the development of our nation. The Maritime Provinces of Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, some of the original partners in Confederation, were the hub of economic activity at that time and, indeed, this was the area where the very concept of Canada was devised. Canada as it exists today can be

June 22, 1983
Government Organization Act, 1983
attributed to Atlantic Canadians and the Fathers of Confederation.
At that time when Atlantic Canada was the economic hub Canadians in that area envisaged a broader sense of participation in those areas which became part of the Dominion of Canada. Atlantic Canadians encouraged the expansion and development of the rest of the country which now makes up Canada. Atlantic Canadians encourage people to become pioneers in a westward expansion throughout Ontario, Quebec, the Prairie Provinces and further.
There is no question that the roots of those Canadians who now inhabit the rest of Canada originated from eastern and Atlantic Canadians, and they contributed greatly to the development of the other parts of Canada. I suggest that those people deserve a particular tribute from Canadians.
Inevitably, there was a price to be paid for the encouragement of this expansion. Indeed, that price has been paid. Unfortunately it has been to the detriment of Atlantic Canada. As a result of the markets which developed in central Canada and the United States, because of their geographic affinity, we have seen a disparity develop in Atlantic Canada that perhaps was not envisaged by the forefathers of our nation.
There evolved an improvement in the transportation system from coast to coast and a promotion of central Canada as a manufacturing base that has been healthy for the nation as a whole. I do not want the House or Canadians to think that Atlantic Canadians begrudge the development of central or western Canada over the lack of development which we have experienced in Atlantic Canada. It is a historical fact that central Canada in particular has developed an economic base as a result of encouragement from Atlantic Canada. Central Canada has claimed a portion of that wealth which might otherwise have developed in Atlantic Canada, the origination of the economic base of this great nation of which we are all proud.
A system of protective barriers has been established over a number of years to protect trade and the establishment of the central manufacturing base in central Canada. I believe this was addressed in the original establishment of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion in 1969. Interestingly enough, that department was established by the very Government which now holds power.
Development in Atlantic Canada has been stymied because of the development in central Canada. There are a number of factors which have caused the slow development of Atlantic Canada, not the least of which is the distance from the Canadian market which that area must have access to in order to grow along with the rest of Canada. We have high transportation costs in moving goods from our manufacturing base in Atlantic Canada to central Canadian markets and beyond. This has resulted in a lack of capital investment in Atlantic Canada. Consequently, we have seen high unemployment and a lack of industrial growth.
Finally, and perhaps most sadly, this has resulted in a dependence on the federal Government which, while necessary,
was not envisaged in the concept Atlantic Canadians held of what Canada would be. Nonetheless, this situation has developed over the years. DREE was established a number of years ago after the Government was made aware of this disparity. The establishment of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion by the Government was indeed a healthy response and one of the few positive actions we have seen the Government take over the years. Unfortunately, it did not last.
As I have stated, DREE was originally established to provide a stimulus to Atlantic and eastern Canada since its mandate included a portion of Quebec, which the present Government has been very quick to recognize over the years. One has only to review the history of the Government to see that Quebec has been the recipient of a great many benefits from the Government. I suggest that can only be expected when one considers that the Province of Quebec has to a great extent encouraged and developed this Government over the years. Nevertheless, it is a national Government which has a responsibility to the entire nation to include those portions of the country that are economically stimulated and those regions which have been economically depreciated. I think it is only fair that as Canadians we expect our government, regardless of which Party it might have as its power base, to include all persons of Canada equally and to look on them with an equally compassionate eye. This Government has fallen down; it has not kept trust with Canadians throughout the country, particularly in terms of being fair and equitable in its proportion of funding.
DREE was a positive step, a positive mesure, a positive department which the Government established, but it did not pursue its purpose; it let it die. In 1970 approximately 2 per cent of federal funding was spent on DREE, which was set up particularly to assist eastern Canada and Atlantic Canada. What have we seen last year and this year? To what degree have we seen DREE deteriorate? This year, its last year of existence, DREE provides only 0.8 per cent of its total spending to help that portion of Canada which it was originally intended to assist. It has long forgotten those portions of Canada which were instrumental in establishing it and in making great this nation of which we are so proud as Canadians.
It is a shame that the Government does not recognize the situation which continues to exist in Atlantic Canada. It fails to recognize that in 1970, only one year after the department was set up, unemployment in Atlantic Canada amounted to 41,000 people. In 1982 the statistics show that unemployment in that area had risen to 135,000, an increase of 229 per cent, in a land where the national average was 168 per cent. The Government tends to prefer to forget about Atlantic Canada. Its unemployment rate in 1970 was 6.2 per cent. In 1982 the unemployment rate had risen to 14.4 per cent. The growth in the unemployment rate in Canada rose by only 5.3 per cent from 1970 to 1982, whereas the average growth in Atlantic Canada was 8.2 per cent.
June 22, 1983

In 1970 after DREE was set up the per capita income of Atlantic Canada was $2,240. In 1982 when the Government decided unilaterally, without consultation with any of its Atlantic Canada partners in Confederation, to destroy the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, the per capita personal income was $9,241. The average throughout the rest of Canada, which the new department will most likely assist, for the Government's own political satisfaction, is now $12,764. Where is the equity? Where is the fairness? Where is the democracy?
