speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1983 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate your acknowledging the significance of the discussion we are having this evening and showing a very distinguished interest for the reorganization of the Department of External Affairs.
The External Affairs Act incorporated in this legislation is simply the legal recognition of changes made last year after the Right Hon. Prime Minister decided to reorganize Government departments and agencies having an economic status. That reorganization has led to major changes in the terms of reference, responsibilities and structure of External Affairs, and these will merely be confirmed by the measure now before us. It is interesting to note that this legislation is the first complete legislative document identifying the role of that Department within the Government organization since 1909. The reorganization which was launched last year is the answer to a variety of questions and considerations raised within the Government. The most obvious, and clearly the driving force behind this reform is the need to adequately promote Canada's economic development. Therefore, the potential for greater economic development being closely linked to the status of our international trade which, as you know, now accounts for 30 per cent of our gross national product, has compelled us to explore a better way not only to maintain but to raise our level of penetration of international markets. That major challenge could simply not be met in any conventional way. The complexity of the markets, the interdependence of the parties concerned, the interconnection between political, economic and trade tensions were calling for concertation and imagination.
Government Organization Act. 1983

Another key objective of the changes brought about in External Affairs was the requirement to bring greater coherence to the range of the Government's policies and programs in the international domain and, in particular, to make trade and economic issues an integral part of our over-all foreign policy. This move responds to the trend which has become increasingly evident of late in international relations whereby political, economic and trade issues have become increasingly intertwined. There is thus a consequent requirement to bring together the various levels of expertise in these areas to deal most effectively with them.
In a similar vein there is a pressing need to ensure that linkages between the domestic and international sectors in terms of the Government's policy development and programs are as effective as possible. Just as the international activities of Government must be reflective of domestic constraints and considerations, so must our domestically focused initiatives be formulated and implemented with a view to their potential international implications.
This requirement is particularly applicable in the case of our own country which is so inextricably tied into the international system, especially in economic terms.
Finally, the changes envisioned reflect the desire to more effectively use and manage resources deployed in support of the Government's international activities. Canada, as is the case with most industrialized countries, has a significant investment in both financial and human terms deployed overseas in our embassies and other offices designed to further the Government's interests and manage the Government's programs. It is incumbent upon us to see to it that this investment is managed in a co-ordinated manner in the interests of economy, efficiency and effectiveness.
The External Affairs Act now being considered by this House responds in a number of ways to the Government's concerns, as I have already outlined, in respect of its international activities. A brief review of the major aspects of the Act will, I am sure, provide a useful indication as to how these concerns are met.

First, under the proposed legislation, the Department of External Affairs will henceforth have three ministers, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister for International Trade and the Minister for External Relations. 1 stress that this is the first time that a particular piece of legislation formally establishes the office of Minister for International Trade, which proves that economic development and particularly the active promotion of our exports are high priorities of this Government. The very existence of the office of Minister for International Trade will ensure that trade and exports will receive the attention they deserve within the administration, and especially around the Cabinet table. It is generally recognized that given the extraordinary opening of

June 22, 1983
Government Organization Act, 1983
Canada onto the world, these three ministers will be able to share the task of looking after our domestic and international interests and ensuring representation of the highest order in the multitude of forums where our country is active.

Second, External Affairs is being given a new mandate in this Act which covers the spectrum of our major international activities. Thus External Affairs will have responsibility for all international trade, economic and political matters as well as our major overseas programs including consular assistance, immigration, development assistance, public and cultural affairs. Of particular importance in this regard is the responsibility External Affairs will have for international trade and economic policy and programs. The assignment of responsibility for international trade to External Affairs is indicative of the Government's concern that trade and economic concerns be better integrated into our over-all foreign policy and, no less, that trade promotion receive a higher profile and priority in our international relations. As well, the general increase in the importance of economic and trade issues in the international environment-including the growing politicization of trade, East-West trade, sanctions, protectionism and the very serious international financial liquidity issues-are such as to require that these issues be dealt with in a broader context which can bring to bear general economic and political considerations in the management of our trade development efforts.
The new mandate for External Affairs will also serve to provide the coherence needed across the range of our international programs and activities in that all of the various strands of our activity-whether political, economic or trade-will be the responsibility of one institution. This centralization of these responsibilities will also provide us with the basis to better manage and co-ordinate the resources the Government deploys in support of its international policies and programs. It will also help to assure that we attain the required balance in our treatment of domestic and international policy issues so that decisions in one area can be taken with a full awareness of the potential implications such decisions may have in other areas.
One further point of interest concerning this Act is that for the first time the authority of our heads of overseas missions is set out in legislation. This, together with the consolidation in External Affairs of the Foreign Service, will provide for a better integration of our overseas operations-whether political, trade, economic, immigration, development assistance or other programs-with consequent advantages for our administration and management of all of our efforts and resources in the international domain.
Before concluding my remarks, I should comment upon the effects which this Act will have for the business community, especially exporters, in Canada. In particular, I would like to deal with those changes which are of special concern to the private sector and, secondly and perhaps somewhat surprisingly, I would like to review a number of aspects of our trade and economic operations with which Members were familiar prior
to the reorganization and which remain largely unchanged in the post-reorganization environment.
Hon. Members will recall that, in large part, the reorganization of the Government was driven by economic development considerations. Foremost amongst these in the case of External Affairs was the desire to see economic and trade considerations being given greater prominence in our foreign policy. More generally, it was also thought that the tranfer of the international trade responsibilities to External Affairs would serve to respond to the growing convergence of political, economic and trade issues in international relations.
The importance of international trade to Canada is well known: our economic well-being is heavily reliant upon our success in developing export markets. Our export capability is dependent not only on factors such as quality of product and financing considerations, but as well on the maintenance of an effective international trading environment. Today we face serious difficulties internationally in terms of potential constraints to facilitating our export growth. Rising protectionist sentiment and policies, the intermingling of political as well as economic considerations in determining commercial transactions, the growing participation of state trading institutions and a variety of other developments have all worked to complicate the international trade and economic environment. Purely export promotion activities are no longer sufficient in and of themselves to ensure that our export potential will be achieved.
The transfer of the trade responsibility to External Affairs has certainly entailed the introduction of some significant changes to our Department and have had a beneficial effect, I believe, on the Government's capacity to deal with international trade and economic policy and issues.
At the ministerial level, the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) will focus his attention on our trade development policies and programs. At the same time, however, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Eachen) will also be actively involved in the development of our over-all international economic and trade efforts. During last year's GATT Ministerial, for example, you may recall that while the Secretary of State for External Affairs chaired the meeting, the Minister of State for International Trade led the Canadian delegation to the meeting. Below the ministerial level the Department's trade and economic specialist are similarly active in the interdepartmental network of policy advisory committees and groups.

All in all, I think one can rightly say that these questions and these policies will receive as much if not more attention within the Department of External Affairs than before the reorganization. Indeed, I would say there are additional benefits to this reform, and I will mention a few.
The consolidation of the foreign service through the transfer of trade officers, in fact through the integration of former employees of Industry, Trade and Commerce into the personnel of External Affairs, had the net result of sensitizing everybody within the Department to trade matters and their
June 22, 1983

peculiarities. I believe there has been a significant improvement in the consistency with which political, economic and trade matters are all taken into account within a global examination of issues, which is beneficial.
Moreover, our trade promotion efforts are aimed at all sectors of the economy, from primary industry to agriculture, from CANDU to Telidon.

I think this might be a useful point at which to set out the aspects of our trade operations which have not changed.
While the Trade Commissioner Service has been consolidated within the Foreign Service, its expertise and experience will be retained. Officers will continue to specialize in trade development work in the Foreign Service whether through assignments abroad or in Canada. Cross-Canada tours by trade officers, before and during overseas assignments will continue as before. As well the practices of maintaining an active secondments program with other parts of the government and, of course, with the private sector remain unchanged.
The programs supporting our export promotion activities with which you may have been familiar in Industry, Trade and Commerce, Madam Speaker, are continuing to function in the same fashion in External Affairs. The program for export market development, our support for fairs and missions, and our support for other promotion projects remain as before reorganization.
Regional trade offices throughout Canada will also be a continuing feature of our trade development activities. These units, staffed by experienced trade personnel, are operating in all of the major regional offices of the new Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. They will continue to provide the same services to the business community as did the regional offices of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
Within the Government, arrangements have been concluded with the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion to ensure the required collaboration between these two departments in a variety of areas so as to retain access to the domestic industrial expertise of that Department. This will include arrangements for an extensive program of secondments between the two Departments in order to ensure that we continue to maintain the required interchange of expertise between our two organizations.
In sum, despite reorganization, a number of key elements of our trade development activities remain as they were. That being said, of course, it should also be stated that reorganization was intended to improve our capabilities in trade policy and development. My own view is that it has and that this will become evident by the Department's performance.
In concluding, Madam Speaker, I should note that much has been made of the new mandate and structure for External Affairs in terms of the contribution it is expected to make to our objectives of national economic development. This is
Government Organization Act, 1983
rightly so, for indeed it is our intention to give economic and trade considerations a central role in our foreign policy and operations. The benefits which we expect to gain, however, are by no means limited to the economic sector. A renewed commitment to comprehensiveness in the formulation of our policy options and operations, coherence in their introduction and consistency in their pursuit can bring us very important advantages across the full range of our international relations.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate being afforded the opportunity to participate in this debate on Bill C-152 which deals with Government re-organization.
As I understand the current re-organization of Government departments, several changes will be occurring that have the possibility of impacting in a positive way on the constituency of Hastings-Frontenac-Lennox and Addington in southeastern Ontario. I say this based on my observation of the current Department of Regional Economic Development that will be abolished in this re-organization. It is the desire of myself and the constituents in my riding that the problems that were never fully dealt with by the old DREE Department will now be addressed.
There are two major thrusts to this Bill: first, the re-organization of Industry, Trade and Commerce, External Affairs and Regional Economic Expansion; and second, expansion of the number of Parliamentary Secretaries and extension of eligibility to include Senators.

June 22, 1983
Government Organization Act, 1983
The Government is re-organized as follows: responsibility for trade is transferred to External Affairs from Industry, Trade and Commerce; a new Department of Regional Industrial Expansion is created out of the existing Departments of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Regional Economic Expansion; the mandate of the Ministry of State for Economic Development is expanded to include regional development; and the MSED thus becomes the Ministry of State for Economic and Regional Development. A new Special Areas Act is established to deal with those DREE responsibilities that are not transferred to the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion.
The potential maximum number of Parliamentary Secretaries will be increased by four and eligibility will be expanded to include Senators. At present, the total number of Parliamentary Secretaries may not exceed the total number of Ministers who receive their salaries under Section 4 of the Salaries Act which, in effect, means Ministers with a department. The formula is expanded to include those who fall under Section 5; that is, Ministers who preside over a Ministry of State.
At present, there are three formal Ministries of State, Economic Development, Social Development and Science and Technology. Not all Ministers of State preside over a Ministry of State. There is, for example, a Minister of State for Trade, but no Ministry of State for Trade.
At the same time this Bill increases by one the number of Ministers who fall under Section 4 of the Salaries Act. Thus, the potential maximum number of Parliamentary Secretaries increases by four. However, should the Government decide to create more Ministries of State, the potential number would increase accordingly as no new legislation is needed to create new Ministries of State.
One of the problems that 1 hope will be addressed is the problem of relevant statistics for determining whether a particular area or region is eligible for assistance. In the northern area of my riding, employment prospects are not particularly encouraging during the best of economic conditions. Many individual communities are dependent on single employment sources, creating a very untenable situation should that employment source dry up. The region, however, has never been able to benefit from direct funding assistance from the federal Government because statistically these certain areas do not appear when calculated with the urban centres of eastern Ontario such as Belleville, Kingston and Ottawa. Therefore, what I would like to see in the new Department of Regional Industrial Expansion that is being created from the existing Departments of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Regional Economic Expansion is a more realistic assessment of those areas and regions within Canada which qualify for assistance but have been unable to obtain it.
I also believe it is very necessary to consult the various levels of Government involved to develop the most effective and comprehensive program for each region. There have been indications that provincial Governments have not been fully consulted about the changes contemplated, and I hope that consultation occurs before this legislation is finalized.
I am concerned about the new Department of Regional Industrial Expansion and the development of new DR IE programs and funding levels. It is my understanding that funding levels for a region will be based on a development index. I have difficulty with this, particularly as this development index proposes to set levels of funding based on a formula that includes percentages of unemployment and income in each census division. This funding scheme then becomes more complicated with its four levels of support and determination of how regions figure in levels of support by how the area scores on the development index.
This formula reminds me of the formula that was developed for the Electoral Boundaries Commission, the use of which somehow afforded one region which had a decrease in population with a net gain of electoral seats at redistribution. That made a mockery of the credo "representation by population". As I mentioned earlier there are several problems with the development index now being proposed in the departmental reorganization.
In the northern area of my federal riding of Hastings-Frontenac-Lennox and Addington, the labour force regions which will help determine the development index have many overlaps in the region. In my constituency the census districts follow the county boundaries. The southern sections of the Counties of Hastings, Lennox and Addington and Frontenac, are very different from the more northerly townships of each of those counties. The southern townships are more populated, more developed and generally enjoy more employment. The northern townships would find that their higher unemployment rate would be distorted by the south.
In Hastings County, the unemployment figure for the City of Belleville will distort the unemployment figure for the northern townships such as Bangor, Wicklow and McClure, Carlow, Monteagle, Herschel and Bancroft 100 miles away. The same will be true for Frontenac County where the unemployment figure for the City of Kingston will distort the unemployment figure for the northern townships in Frontenac County such as Palmerston North and South Canonto, Clarendon and Miller and Barrie Townships. The situation will repeat itself in Lennox and Addington County also.
The proposed alternative of trying to estimate unemployment rates for census districts individually will lead to a further accuracy problem. This has been pointed out to me in the size of the survey of the labour force, in that the smaller the survey, the higher the degree of inaccuracy. Even when the amount of unemployment is determined, it only tells part of the story. There are many people in areas who have given up looking for work because they know there is none available. The Government's proposal does not consider these individuals.
Finally, I would like to mention the second measure of the development index, that of income. The proposal is to use as our income measure that of personal income in a census district based on taxation data. In this accounting, there is the
June 22, 1983

problem of time. Tax data that will become available will be several years old by the time it is published. In July of 1982 a major employer in the northern area of Hastings County shut down. By using the federal Government's proposed method of accounting, this major shift in the income pattern in the local economy will not be available until 1985 at the earliest, clearly years out of date.
The development index formula has many problems, however the one that is most serious is the fact that the formula will not be put into law. The possibility of year to year political tampering by the Minister in charge renders all the departmental re-organization of regional industrial expansion virtually ineffective. That does not suggest the re-organization will have any effectiveness.
Unfortunately, the major thrust in past instances of Canadian regional policy has been to support Government intervention, and the interference of the operation of natural market forces in a particular region, when and where it was politically advantageous to do so and not in consideration of those regions where need had been demonstrated. This fact becomes more painfully evident when one examines where DREE moneys have been allocated since the inception of the Department in 1969. The Province of Quebec has received $1.5 billion, $900 million more than the next most highly funded DREE Province. In the 1980-81 fiscal year Quebec received $168 million compared to $34 million in Ontario, which has a higher population, $17 million in Alberta and $38 million in British Columbia to name a few other Provinces.
We were never opposed to the goals and objectives of regional development, only to the partisan political tampering which has distorted the role of the old DREE and which, if the proper parliamentary control is not maintained, will hamper the effectiveness of the new DRIE re-organization.
Early in committee I was able to ask a number of questions to officials about DRIE. While much was said of the major commitment to the Ontario region by DRIE, no information was forthcoming about the number of projects or the specific areas in which projects were being developed. I am concerned about the lack of information available to MPs about the operation of DRIE.
In many of the areas of the less developed regions of Canada, historical as well as economic factors are responsible for poor economic growth. In the same vein, in the relatively prosperous Province of Ontario there are areas of economic distress. The federal Government should be focusing its efforts less on regional disparities and more on the areas within each Province throughout Canada that could benefit from some form of economic assistance.
It is also evident that the solutions that must be developed must be individually matched to the distinctive need within each area of all regions.
I hope we will see in this new Department a definite approach that will define the economic potential of a less developed region as opposed to the creation of a make-work project that provides no long-term lasting benefit to that
Government Organization Act, 1983
region. While I do not believe this request is impossible I am not so sure this Government has the will to implement it.
Over the past few years, federal policies and programs with regard to regional development have undergone major changes. It would appear that the concern with sharing the economic benefits of Confederation more equally among all the regions of the country is being replaced by an overwhelming preoccupation with the ways and means of stimulating national economic growth. While this may be appropriate, given the current problems of the national economy, it should be clearly understood that the changes in federal policy, particularly as they affect the flow of funds into poorer regions, could have very serious short-run consequences for individuals and provincial Governments and ultimately on the national economy.
Some of the many areas which now seem to be affected by this change in policy are as follows. First, the federal Government is seeking to restrict the transfer of funds to provincial Governments for some programs, such as established program funding and equalization, through changes in the terms of the programs or limiting increases.
The new Industrial and Regional Development Program, IRDP, will form the basis of DRIE assistance. Firms anywhere in Canada can qualify for assistance which varies in degree according to a development index calculated for each of Canada's 260 census divisions. The index will be based on unemployment rate, income, and the fiscal capacity of each Province, although the relative weighting of each of these components has not yet been announced. Based on the value of the index, each census division will qualify for increasing levels of assistance according to its relative disparity on a four-tiered scale.
Was DREE a failure? I do not think so. However, to the best of my knowledge there have been no studies to assess the effectiveness of DREE programs in meeting established objectives. Certainly DREE had its faults as well as its strengths and we would welcome the prospect of a more sophisticated program appropriate to today's economic environment.
The new IRDP represents a shift in direction from previous development initiative and has been a cause of concern for APEC. It may be that some of these misgivings may evaporate as more aspects of the program become known. However, some of my preliminary concerns are that some of the previous industrial development programs, such as EDP, were unsuited to the needs of the smaller manufacturing companies. The creation of a tiered development index alone is unlikely to increase their application.
The new proposals do not appear to recognize the need for a concentrated approach to economic development beyond the boundary of a single census division. As a consequence, some of the new programs could have limited application in the smaller census divisions in Canada with their limited industrial base and weak infrastructure.

June 22, 1983
Government Organization Act, 1983
Depending on the final form of area indices, the proposed incremental incentives appear inadequate to influence decisions on plant location if that is the policy objective. Policy initiatives of the past have not succeeded in achieving this goal and we now see changes in direction.
Although details for implementation of new policies have not yet been made clear, it is essential to voice these concerns. Further disclosures on the nature of the new economic development instruments will allow a much more specific focus on the issues.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Maltais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1983 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be able to take part in the debate this evening on the second reading stage of Bill C-152, where it concerns the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. I would like to start by emphasizing that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has existed in its present form for 15 years, and I believe that Canadians from all parts of the country will acknowledge that this Department has done a great deal for the development of certain parts of Canada and especially, I think, in Eastern Canada and in other parts of Ontario which have been able to take advantage of the various programs and mechanisms made available to the various regions.
Madam Speaker, when we look at Bill C-152 which provides for the creation of a Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, we must listen to both the heart and the mind. I think that initially, we do feel sad at the thought that a department like DREE which has been doing excellent work for over 15 years, will now have to change directions and be restructured, and consequently, it is quite legitimate to expect that there will be some resistance to change, which will be normal and acceptable, but still hard to justify if we were to focus only on emotional considerations. I think we must go beyond that to seek formulas that will do a lot more for the future and will help us meet a host of technological and economic challenges. What should be said first of all, Madam Speaker, is that the new Department that has just been created . . . and here we must support and add to efforts that were made in the past, and not denigrate or simply abolish what was set up in 1969. On the contrary! I think it is normal for a Government to want to review such programs from time to time. I am convinced that after 15 years it was time this program was updated and revamped.
Madam Speaker, what exactly does this revamping of the former DREE and the former Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, propose to do? The aim is basically to be much closer to the regions than these departments were before, without necessarily being restricted to providing service or support through participation in studies of various industries and various factories, since it intends to be more concrete and more effective as far as marketing, modernization and research
are concerned. I think that is very important, because these are areas that have perhaps not been neglected but not given as much attention as they should have received under the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. By restructuring the Department with Industry, Trade and Commerce and the former DREE department, what we are actually aiming at is to put two tools in the same box to ensure that all our human resources that want to help this country's economic development can do so as a team. That, Madam Speaker, is the purpose of the amalgamation of the former Department of Regional Economic Expansion with that of Industry, Trade and Commerce. It is a fact that at an early stage, we were wondering whether the proposed tool was potentially the best. It is also a fact that with changes such as this, people wonder just how the new set up will be an improvement over the previous one. Of course, as was indicated by the previous speaker, we do wonder whether or not we are taking a big chance. I think that we probably are just taking a chance as with any other change, but one which will bring about new initiatives, while keeping the expertise accumulated over the past 15 years.
I think this is very important. And when he appeared before various committees, the Minister indicated most emphatically that there was not intention of taking away resources at the ministerial level or to lower the profile of the people directly involved in regional economic expansion. I think that on this we should take the Minister's word for it and rely on it, for the Minister's major concern is to ensure that the decision-making process is not merely at the central level, but also at the regional level.
I can say this with considerable pride, Madam Speaker, for the North Shore has benefited to a large extent from the various programs implemented by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. So has Eastern Canada, and people are quite satisfied with what has already been done. Most of the time, people complained that the decisions concerning industries, corporations, small and medium-size businesses, which were supposed to be responsible and wise, taken following an in-depth study, were made either in the National Capital or in major cities where the regional offices were situated which made it very difficult for small and medium-size businesses to obtain assistance at the local level.
Accordingly the new department effectively anticipates that we will be ever more present in the regions and in larger numbers to comply with the wishes of those directly involved in industry and development. Even if the parties opposite have some reservations, amendments will probably be introduced in Committee of the Whole and already as far as improvements are concerned we could perhaps make sure that we have just one wicket precisely because of the various economic needs identified by the decisions-makers because with DREE there was one major problem. When a product had to be marketed or developed or still when a new economic activity, had to be organized DREE would say: "Listen, we are only limited to
June 22, 1983

that part of the job, the other part comes under the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. On the other hand this Department would answer that from now on people would have to deal with the Department of External Affairs when they needed to investigate markets abroad and there were all sorts of very specialized fields, the co-ordination of which proved to be quite a challenge.
Now that the Department has been reorganized, many of the problems usually encountered in the consideration of issues have been eliminated, and still more, we will be taking advantage of an expanded amount of expertise at the regional level. We will gain considerable time in the evaluation of issues and we will possess a mass of combined knowledge and as a result those who want to use our services will no longer be discouraged. Members from all sides of the House will note that when we have to deal with various departments, we are often shifted from one department to another and regularly told that this branch of a department works on this aspect of an issue while that branch of another department deals with that economic aspect. It proved very hard to obtain any information so that in that respect we will have made substantial progress.
And what does Bill C-152 provide in Part II?
Powers and duties are granted to the Minister. I think that this again is very clear. It is provided that the powers, duties and functions of the Minister generally extend to very specific sectors-manufacturing industries and service industries. Previously I think they were somewhat limited as far as services were concerned. We will be involved with regional industrial expansion. This means that for Members from this side of the House and even from the other side who had reservations with regard to the involvement of the new Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, the concern will remain the same, Madam Speaker. We are going to be very close to the regions, but also we will have more personnel to work directly. So for people who do have doubts in that respect, the Act actually provides for a regional presence. We are going to look after tourism. It is a well-known fact that today tourism in some Provinces is a key activity, and Canada is increasingly anxious to see all our tourist trade potential represented on the world scene. I would simply like to point out that recently one of the tourist treasures of the North Shore, the Mingan Archipelego, was added to Canada's heritage.
Often reference is made to small and medium businesses, and often they directly benefit from the assistance given to large corporations. Mention should be made of the various aircraft and shipbuilding contracts. Small and medium businesses supply larger contractors or shipyards. So these small and medium businesses will benefit, as well as interprovincial trade. Reference has often been made to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion as if that Department's operations were only restricted to the Maritimes or Quebec. But the
Government Organization Act, 1983
aim must be an increasingly strengthened internal trade within Canada, and the powers and duties of the Minister are set out as very specific and well-defined functions.
And there is more to be found in that legislation when you look at it more closely. The following is provided in Section 5.1:
(a)	promote the establishment, growth and efficiency of manufacturing, processing, service and tourist industries in all regions of Canada, contribute to the sound development and productivity of Canadian industries generally and foster the expansion of trade in Canada-
Needless to say, at the last Progressive Conservative Convention this was one of the major points that were emphasized. It raises the whole question of productivity in larger industries as well as in small and medium businesses in Canada.
It is therefore my view that the Opposition parties will have to admit that this has been in preparation for quite some time in order to have a Department that will better meet future challenges, and this in no way conflicts with the principles which they are putting forward. On the contrary, this emphasizes and illustrates the extent to which the productivity of Canadian industries must be increased while certain leading and traditional sectors of our economy are upgraded. The Bill provides, among other things, in paragraph (b), that the Minister shall:
(b)	assist investors in the location of industries in a manner that is consistent with the needs of the investors and federal regional and industrial development policies-
In the past, major industries were often developed in large urban centres and marginal areas were left with the small businesses. However, at the present time and according to the various scenarios which the Department will introduce in the near future by regulation, all regions will have equal opportunities to attract major processing industries so that they will not always lag behind the large centres and large areas will not be more developed than others. Equal opportunities will be provided to those regions that are now known as underdeveloped. That is the important thing! Central Canada may have developed much more quickly than other regions, but the time has come to try to strike a balance.
These normal and legitimate concerns are shared by both sides of the House, and I believe that they had to be met by such a piece of legislation.
In Subclause (d) of this Bill, we also find that the Minister shall, and I quote:
(d) develop and carry out programs related to his powers, duties and functions, of a national and regional character, including programs and projects to
(i) promote and assist product and process development-
I heard that during the leadership campaign of the Progressive Conservative Party, Madam Speaker, and I have often heard NDP members say the same thing, and quite rightly.
As an exporting country, Canada must have well-organized high technology industries.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1983 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce set up the Canadian Industrial Renewal Board, or CIRB, to try to find means of increasing production and reducing costs to promote exports in so-called soft traditional sectors, such as the textile industry.
In addition, I think it is about time we developed new products in Canada, because all our young people are looking to microprocessors and high technology. The technological revolution may be just another phrase for us, but it is a reality in other countries. It is therefore important for a Department to be able to coordinate such activities. In the past, development meant research centres under the jurisdiction of other Departments than that of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and it was the responsibility of External Affairs to find new markets, but there had never been an economically-oriented Department working in very close co-operation with businessmen and businesswomen and able to point the way to new markets and new opportunities. All these activities will now be regrouped under three Departments: External Affairs, Regional Industrial Expansion and the Department which will be responsible for marketing. That is what we had to do, and under this legislation, I think that we shall have to see to it that there will be a single government agency in the various regions. I think this is an excellent piece of legislation, to the extent that it will bring us closer to the people and that we will not forever have to give other departments the information required to enable the people to act knowledgeably and responsibly. In addition, Madam Speaker, other duties of the Department include, and I quote:
(e) provide support services for industrial and trade development, including information, import analysis and traffic services-
Everyone will admit that the last consideration is of major importance to the country, the question of traffic services. Most of the time we do experience difficulties due to the vastness of our country and the lack of modern railway facilities. Besides, let us admit it, the high cost of transportation is often the only thing which prevents our merchants, businessmen and businesswomen from moving throughout the country to sell their goods-prohibitive transportation costs. The question of traffic services is basic in this Bill and we will have to make sure that it is more than pious wishes, that it becomes a reality so that we will be able to transport our own products from the Atlantic to the Pacific and, increasingly, from the Arctic to our southern borders. Afterwards we will have to make sure that with outstanding transporters such as Air Canada and CP Air we will take our goods to Europe. There are markets but we must look beyond North America. Granted, the United States remain our main trading partner, but we must seek new outlets in China and Japan because our country is blessed with natural resources. Japan, with her huge population, must protect every single tree which grows on her islands. Europeans are now looking for lumber producing countries. Canada is a country which can meet those needs, but we must process our lumber right here. Transportation should not however be an obstacle to our trade, but it is now one of of our
major difficulties. By combining the Department of External Affairs with the former Department of Regional Economic Expansion and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, I think we have found a major lever to ensure Canada's economic recovery and diversification.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, I should like to say that we will need more that economic recovery programs. We will be successful if all Canadians, men and women alike, are truly motivated not only politically, but individually and personally. I am convinced that we will have a few false starts at the beginning, because the whole apparatus will have to be put to the test, and that is to be expected. A number of public servants will be frustrated because many of them do have soft jobs. We are here to serve the public, find new formulas and make sure that we do not fall prey to a kind of lethargic sleep. This Bill will shake up some people, but that is our job and it is important that we do it well. Knowing as I do the new Leader of the Opposition, I am almost certain that he will be tempted to repeat word for word what I have just said. The major hazard facing the Leader of the Opposition-I do know him well

is that he is a good Liberal. I have always thought that he was a Liberal who had lost his way, so those who are more conservative that progressive should be on their toes! To conclude my remarks, Madam Speaker, I will say that this legislation is welcome. Like any Hon. Member on both sides of the House, I have a few legitimate reservations. But let us give a chance to the department before destroying it and let us wait and see what the results are. In addition, I am convinced that these provisions will benefit all Canadians. Nothing prevents us from reviewing the new legislation every year, for it is wrong to make changes in our laws only every 15 years. It is about time as well that the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce stop patronizing, leaving unimportant matters to small regions, and that we strike together, to achieve a really balanced development of our economy.

Member hope to convince the Canadian people that this is a major bill or that the policies of this Government are working?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would like to point out one thing to the Hon. Member. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, now we are all really confused. It was not my intention to spend too much of my 20 minutes on the new Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, except to say that there is nothing that it will do which could not have been done by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. Indeed, it rather narrows it. The Hon. Member for Manicouagan (Mr. Maltais) suggested that now the new Department would be able to really seek out industry. That was what DREE was supposedly to do, primarily. There were other kinds of economic expansion for DREE, but fundamentally it was an attempt to have industries locating in slow growth or less developed areas. Therefore, it is pretty much of a manicured type of thing.
The main reason the new Department of Regional Industrial Expansion has been created is the wish of the Government to break up the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce

June 22, 1983
Government Organization Act, 1983
and to put Industry in with the new Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, and to put Trade and Commerce in with the Department of External Affairs. I am pretty sure that is what the Government is doing, despite the Hon. Member assuring me that that is what it was not doing. I am sure he thought that that is what it was not doing.
None of the relevant Ministers in the new Department of External Affairs are here tonight. One of them peeked in for a moment and left. I guess he really does not care what is happening to this hydra which is being created in the Department of External Affairs. However, I think one of the real worries of the new Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Lumley), who is here tonight, would be that while there may have been an absence of co-ordination in the past between DREE and Industry, the absence of co-ordination in the future between Industry, Trade and Commerce will be enormous and probably far more serious.
Some of the officials to whom we spoke in the Committee on External Affairs did point out the great difficulty they would have in Trade and Commerce, in that section of the new Department of External Affairs, because they would not have as intimate and close a relationship with their domestic industrial base and their clients, their constituents, so to speak, whereas when it was all together in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, people engaged in export promotion, trade and so on, did have a pretty close tie-in with the industrial sectors of the country which they were anxious to see becoming more competitive on the world market.
Therefore, one of the toughest problems the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion will face is the very tie-in with one's industrial contituency that the old Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce had. I am sure that he will agree that that will be a problem. However, I want to talk primarily about the Department of External Affairs Act because it is an abomination. There are many parts to it which ought to be repealed. Let me name a few of those parts.
This Act, originally Bill C-123, was given first reading almost a year ago on June 30, 1982. The Government has had all that time in which it could have seen the inadequacies and horrendous mistakes made in the section headed Department of External Affairs Act and made changes.
It has made other changes. It withdrew the regional incentives part from the original Bill C-123 which the Minister has now introduced separately. The Government has withdrawn the financial administration part which will be dealt with separately. While the Government has been dealing with this hydra-headed monster, I see that it did not remove the section entitled the Parliamentary Secretary's Act. I will return to that question. Yet it did not make any changes whatsoever to Part I which is the Department of External Affairs Act. As an example of the inadequacies of this Bill, we first have the Secretary of State for External Affairs as we do today. We then have two additional Ministers, the Minister for International Trade and the Minister for External Relations, both of
whom carry out their duties under the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
The powers, duties and functions of the Secretary of State for External Affairs are outlined in detail in Clause 11. The powers, duties and functions of the Minister for International Trade are outlined in Clause 12. However, there is absolutely nothing about the duties and powers of the third Minister, the Minister for External Relations. To bring forward a statute creating a new Minister for External Relations and having nothing in the statute about his powers and duties is, to me, absolutely incredible.
I have been trying to understand this Bill since it has been presented as a fait accompli and the Minister for External Relations has already been operating. 1 have been trying to understand what he is doing. I have read the press releases and have listened to him in the House. If the abysmal speech he made the other day when debating the Cruise missile testing during Opposition day was an example of what he is doing, then I am even more confused about what his role is supposed to be.
I would say that there is no way a statute creating a new Minister which does not indicate what his duties are should go through the House. Therefore, I would suggest that the first action should be to abolish that position. I will return to the issue of international trade, but I believe that we should abolish the position of Minister for External Relations. I hope that will be done in Committee of the Whole. Indeed, this Bill should go to the relevant standing committees because it needs much more attention than can possibly be given in Committee of the Whole.
Let me deal with the undersecretaries. We have always had an undersecretary of state for External Affairs in Canada who is the deputy head of the Department. We will now have three associate undersecretaries, positions which in fact already exist. As I said, this legislation is a fait accompli. We have talked to those undersecretaries in committee. One position is for an associate undersecretary to the Minister of State for International Trade, who is a deputy. The second is to be a deputy to the Minister in charge of foreign policy. Incidentally, he is referred to here as the Minister for Foreign Policy and elsewhere he is called the Minister for External Relations. The Government has not even figured out what the title will be. Since we do not know what the Minister will do, how are we to know what the deputy is supposed to do? Therefore, that section must be abolished when we deal with this Bill in committee.
The reason that I am looking at the Hon. Minister for the new Department of Regional Industrial Expansion is that I know he shares my concerns. He just has not been heard in Cabinet, which I find amazing, because he should be heard.
The Minister and the House will also know that there is a third associate undersecretary of state who is to be "the coordinator of international economic relations." He will have the rank and status of a deputy head of the Department. I have not been able to find an explanation here or anywhere else as to what he will do.

Another fascinating problem from the point of view of a student of public administration is that each of these Ministers, the Secretary of State and the other two Ministers have an undersecretary or deputy and an associate. It is not clear whether they respond to their own Minister in the case of the deputies or whether they respond to the undersecretary of state, who then responds to the Secretary of State who, in turn, informs the other Ministers what it is they have been responding about. There is simply no clarification in this area at all. Other Members here who were at the committee will agree that we tried to clarify that in committee. The Government is going to establish committees to help it decide who will respond to whom and why. As I say, any student of public administration looking at this monster would have a field day. If I only had an hour I could go on.

I will not go on about that subject or the McDougall report at this time because the External Affairs Act does not deal with assistant undersecretaries. I am simply illustrating the fact that this entire measure is in a very sorry state. People's responsibilities are overlapping and they are having great difficulty in determining who is supposed to be doing what.
As I have suggested, we must abolish the position of Minister of External Relations, his deputy and the co-ordinator for international economic relations. No one knows what he is supposed to do.
I would like to proceed to the question of the division of Industry, Trade and Commerce and including Trade and Commerce in External Affairs. I realize that time should be given to determine how it would work out but one of my reservations, and indeed that of the Deputy Minister as expressed in committee, is over breaking the linkage between industry in this country and trade and commerce that this development will involve. I am also concerned because I think it is better to have trade and commerce quite separately represented at Cabinet. People may say that the Minister is
Government Organization Act, 1983
separate from the Secretary of State, but that is not entirely so. The Minister should not only have close links with industry in the country but remain quite separate and equal in status. I would sooner have that than have him occupy a position in the Department of External Affairs which would not be as strong if he were an equal, but nevertheless will be strong enough for him to inject into the foreign policies of the country an extremely strong bias on the trade side.
Canada, as we have said a million times, is a trading nation. Therefore we must have a very strong trade side, strong export promotion, and so on, in the Government of Canada. But it would be a grave mistake when we consider the kinds of foreign policy initiatives which Canada has taken in the past and will take in the future-Canada may not be taking many today but it is taking a few; it has suddenly realized that Central America is there, for example-to put great emphasis upon our external appearance and thrust into the promotion of trade and commerce. We may very seriously undermine other policy directions, whether they be in human rights, peacekeeping or whatever the Department of External Affairs ordinarily conducts.
This may percolate through the whole Department. There are absolutely first class trade commissioners in the trade commissioner service; as we all know, a great many of them are first class. They are not primarily, nor should they be, people who have to embrace the totality of Canadian foreign policy. Yet, under the planned administration of the new Department of External Affairs, including Trade and Commerce, as I understand it from talking with many of the officials, they will in fact be one of the interchangeable streams within the Department which will have to take on many other functions than the trade promotion function. Because of their strength as trade people, I am not sure that they are really able to be, with a few exceptions, capable of a broad representation of Canadian foreign policy rather than simply Canadian trade abroad. I am worried that they will not do that.
Ideally, I would like us to drop this part of the Bill for both the reasons I have given. It seems to me that this reorganization will not do anything which the Department of Regional Economic Expansion could not have done. It would remove the link which I think is important between industry, trade and commerce and will give the whole Department of External Affairs, or a large part of it, a very trade and commercially oriented salience. This would be very seriously to the detriment of the salience of the Department which most of us have seen in the past and would like to continue to see. Therefore, this means a very major change. In fact, it pretty well revokes Part I and Part II. I guess we will just revoke them. That leaves us with Part IV, which was Part VI in the original Bill.
It is obvious that Part IV cannot remain. It would be very condescending of me even to address this since I am sure it is

I am very concerned about the whole problem of co-ordinating. One speaker on the Government side mentioned there could be seconding. Mir. Maurice A. Dionne (Northumberland-Miramichi):
Madam Speaker, I would like to spend a few minutes dealing with the second part of this Bill which creates the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. It will replace the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. When you look at in terms of names, it does not make a lot of difference. However, in terms of how the delivery system will work, it can make a great deal of difference.
The most redeeming feature is that we have a bit of hindsight because the Bill is being enacted retroactively, after the reorganization has occurred. That is not an entirely unusual situation. It has occurred with almost every new Government that has been elected in this nation. Another redeeming feature is the person who occupies the position of Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion. To date he has shown that he is sensitive to the regions of Canada and to the industrial expansion of those regions. He is the only good reason I can think of for supporting this Bill because I have seen him in action.
I was very much opposed to the idea when it first appeared. However, I have had opportunity to deal with the results of the reorganization. I believe we can have a better delivery system with fewer encumbrances. The Government of Canada will be able to act in a much more expeditious and reasonable manner, without having to take into consideration the political machinations to which the Government of Canada was almost continuously subjected by the Provinces.
In New Brunswick, under DREE we had a number of development agreements covering various parts of the Province. It made the Province look somewhat like a checkerboard or hopscotch board. You could jump from one part of an area to another which had the ability to take advantage of the incentives. Two miles away, and maybe even half a mile away, there were no incentives available.
Government Organization Act, 1983
I want to express the hope that the intention of this Bill is to make it possible for a much better delivery of the economic incentives that the Government is prepared to offer to those companies, firms or individuals that are prepared to take some risk in establishing industries of one type or another, industries that will employ local people and produce goods locally and which will improve the industrial base and the ability to market in those areas of the country that to date have been left behind.
We know that the vast majority of industrial activity in this country is centred in Ontario. I do not believe there is anything wrong with Ontario being industrialized. However, there is a great deal wrong if there are only one or two areas of the country that can be industrialized. I believe that this and any successive Government must have as its prime responsibility redressing the problem of employment opportunities through industrial development in every part of this nation. No part of this nation needs that more than the Gaspe and the Atlantic Provinces.
It is convenient for a lot of people to forget that when Confederation came about, the Atlantic region was the industrialized area of Canada. It is very convenient for Deputy Ministers who spend all or most of their time in Ottawa to forget that. It will be very difficult for this Minister to forget it because I intend to remind him constantly that we were industrialized. I do not claim that the policy of Macdonald was wrong. I cannot remember any experiences from that era. However, the industrial policy, the centralization policies of his Government, destroyed the industries of Atlantic Canada. We must make every possible effort to rebuild that.
The Government of Canada has a very special responsibility to see that every possible incentive is put in place for any individual, industry or corporation wishing to establish. I would go further than that. I would say that the Government of Canada must use a great deal of persuasion to insist that industry in this country in its expansion plans looks at areas of the country other than southwestern Ontario and the Montreal region. It is absolutely imperative that Canadians who live in the rest of Canada should be able to take part in the new industrial growth, the new technological growth, the new scientific growth and the new educational growth in the country. To do otherwise would be an abrogation of the responsibility of the Government, and I hope that that will be taken seriously, Madam Speaker.
